en: The Scripture of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, Scroll One.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha, during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
1. Chapter One: The Introduction Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of sixty-four thousand bhikṣus.

There were seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were well known to the public; they had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence as well as various samādhis, were unhindered in their supernormal powers, were skillfully able to comprehend the true nature of all phenomena, and had all attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Their names were:

Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Ratnapāṇi Kumārabhūta, Ratnakūṭa Kumārabhūta, Ratnamudrāhasta Kumārabhūta, Ratnaśrī Kumārabhūta, Gaganagañja Kumārabhūta, Citta-utpāda-dharmacakra-pravartana Kumārabhūta, Jālinīprabha Kumārabhūta, Sarvakleśanirghātana Kumārabhūta, Sarvadharmaparityāga Kumārabhūta, Guṇakośa Kumārabhūta, Kusumavyūha Kumārabhūta, Siṃha Kumārabhūta, Candraprabha Kumārabhūta, Āśayagarbha Kumārabhūta, Suvyūha Kumārabhūta; as well as the sixteen virtuous youths, such as Bhadrapāla and the others:

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas Bhadrapāla, Ratnakūṭa, Jyotirasa, Indradeva, Varuṇadeva, Suvikrāntaśakti, Mahāmati, Viśeṣamati, Vardhamānamati, Susaṃprasthitamati, Amoghadarśin, Anikṣiptadhura, Aparihīṇamati, Nāyaka, Sūryagarbha, and Dharaṇīdhara—these and other such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas numbered seventy-two thousand.

The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, and the rest, including the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Yāma heaven, Tuṣita heaven, Nirmāṇarati heaven, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, as well as Brahmā-rāja and the other Brahmā devas;
together with immeasurable others—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all gathered there in great numbers.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly who paid him respectful homage as he preached the Dharma.

Then, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet. Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he shook this trichiliocosm to inspire and awaken the entire assembly, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask the Buddha a few questions; if the Buddha permits me, I shall venture to seek his instruction.
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha, "Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you so as to gladden your heart."
Thereupon, having received permission, Jālinīprabha was filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body surpass the radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of suns and moons."
I reflected to myself:
"If there are sentient beings who are able to see the Buddha’s body, that is truly rare!
I further reflected:
"If there are sentient beings who are able to see the Buddha's body, it is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata!
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha: "So it is, so it is!"
As you have said, if the Buddha did not apply his majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), sentient beings would be unable to see the Buddha’s body, nor would they be able to question him.
Jālinīprabha, you should know this!
The Tathāgata has a light named "Tranquil Adornment"; if there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they are able to behold the Buddha’s body without their faculty of sight being impaired.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has a light named "Fearless Eloquence"; if there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they are able to question the Tathāgata with inexhaustible eloquence.

Moreover, the Tathāgata has a light named "Gathering All Roots of Goodness"; if there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they are able to question the Tathāgata regarding the karmic causes and conditions of the deeds of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Pure Adornment; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to ask the Tathāgata about the causes and conditions of the conduct of Śakra, Lord of Devas.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Attaining Sovereignty; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to ask the Tathāgata about the causes and conditions of the conduct of Brahmā, King of Devas.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Free from Affliction; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to ask the Tathāgata about the path practiced by those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Skillful Detachment"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the path practiced by Pratyekabuddhas.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Benefiting All-Knowledge"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the Mahāyāna Buddha-activities.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Benefiting upon Arrival"; when the Buddha comes or goes, the radiance from beneath his feet causes those sentient beings who encounter it to be reborn in the heavens at the end of their lives.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "All-Adorned"; when the Buddha enters a city and emits this radiance, sentient beings who encounter it attain joy and bliss, all manner of ornamental articles adorn the city, and treasure troves emerge from the earth within the city.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Vibrating"; by means of this light, the Buddha can shake immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Producing Joy"; by means of this light, the Buddha can extinguish the suffering and affliction of sentient beings in the hells.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Supreme Compassion"; by means of this light, the Buddha is able to cause animals not to harm one another.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Cool Refreshment"; by means of this light, the Buddha is able to extinguish the heat-afflictions of hunger and thirst among the hungry ghosts.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Luminous Purity"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables the blind to see.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Attentive Hearing"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings who are deaf to hear.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Shame and Remorse"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings who are deranged to attain correctness.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Cessation and Rest"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings to abandon the ten unwholesome paths and dwell securely in the ten wholesome paths.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Departing from Evil"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings with false views to all attain right view.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Able to Renounce"; by means of this light, the Buddha can destroy the hearts of stinginess and greed in sentient beings, causing them to practice giving.

Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Free from Affliction and Heat"; by means of this light, the Buddha can cause sentient beings who have violated the precepts to all attain the keeping of the precepts.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called Beneficial and Peaceful; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to all practice patience.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called Diligent Cultivation; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings who are indolent to all practice diligence.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called Single-Mindedness; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings with distracted thoughts to all attain meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named "Capable of Liberation," by which the Buddha enables sentient beings who are ignorant and deluded to all attain wisdom;
likewise, there is a Tathāgata light named "Pure," by which the Buddha enables sentient beings who lack faith to all attain pure faith;
and likewise, there is a Tathāgata light named "Capable of Sustaining," by which the Buddha enables sentient beings who have heard little to all attain extensive learning.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Dignified Conduct"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables shameless sentient beings to attain a sense of shame and remorse.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Tranquility"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings with excessive desire to sever their lustful cravings.
Again, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Joy"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables sentient beings with excessive anger to sever their hatred.
Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named Illumination; by means of this light, the Buddha can cause sentient beings with excessive delusion to sever their ignorance.
Again, there is a Tathāgata light named Pervasive Movement; by means of this light, the Buddha can cause sentient beings with balanced dispositions to sever their balanced afflictions.
Again, there is a Tathāgata light named Manifesting All Colors; by means of this light, the Buddha can cause all sentient beings to see the Buddha’s body in its immeasurable varieties of color.

Jālinīprabha, you should know that even if the Tathāgata were to spend an eon, or slightly less than an eon, explaining the names and the power and function of this radiance, they could not be fully exhausted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha,
saying: “It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
The body of the Tathāgata is a treasury of immeasurable and boundless radiance, and the skillful means of his preaching the Dharma are likewise inconceivable.
World-Honored One!
Since ancient times, I have never heard the name of this radiance.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there are bodhisattvas who hear the name of this light and their faith becomes pure, they shall all attain such a body of light.
World-Honored One!

We pray that you will today emit the light that invites bodhisattvas, so that bodhisattvas from other regions who are skilled in posing difficult questions, upon seeing this light, may resolve to come to this Sahā world.

At that time, having accepted the request of Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a radiance that illuminated this trichiliocosm and extended throughout the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Thereupon, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas from all directions, having seen this light, all came to this Sahā world.

At that time, seventy-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands to the east, there was a land named Pure and Clean; its Buddha was named Sūryacandraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides in that Buddha-land.
There was a bodhisattva Brahmā named Siyi (Suvikrānta), who dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
Having seen this light, he went to the presence of the Buddha Candrasūryaprabha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to go to the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha to behold him, make offerings to him, and draw near to him to receive his instruction;
that Buddha likewise wishes to see us.
That Buddha said to him:
"Go then, Brahmā! Now is the very time!"
In that Sahā world-system, there are several thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas gathered together; you should travel through that land by means of these ten dharmas. What are the ten?
Regarding both slander and praise, the mind neither increases nor decreases;
hearing of good or evil, the mind makes no distinction;
toward all, whether foolish or wise, one regards them equally with a heart of compassion.
Toward the classes of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—one’s intention is always impartial;
toward both contemptuous insults and respectful offerings, one’s mind remains without duality;
and regarding the failings of others, one perceives no fault.
Seeing various vehicles, one should realize they are all the One Vehicle;
hearing of the three evil realms, one should not be startled or afraid;
and toward all bodhisattvas, one should conceive the thought that they are Tathāgatas.
"The Buddha appears in the five turbidities; one should conceive a sense of rare wonder. Brahmā!
You should travel through that world by means of these ten dharmas."
The Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not dare to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata; what I am able to practice, the Buddha himself knows.”
"Now, you should travel to that world by means of these ten dharmas, practicing with single-minded devotion.
At that time, various bodhisattvas in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryaprabha addressed their Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I have attained a great benefit, for I am not born among such evil sentient beings.
That Buddha told him:
"Good son, do not speak such words!"

Why is this? If a bodhisattva were to practice the pure conduct of brahmacarya in this land for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, it would not equal the merit of one who, in that land, maintains a mind free from anger and obstruction from morning until the meal; the latter's merit is superior.
At that moment, twelve thousand bodhisattvas together with the Brahma-king Viśeṣacintin arrived, and they spoke these words:
“We, too, wish to travel to that world by means of these ten dharmas in order to see Śākyamuni Buddha.”

Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, suddenly vanished from that buddha-field. In the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm, they arrived at the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world and stood to one side.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:
"Do you see this Brahmā Viśeṣacintin?
[He replied: "Indeed, I do."
"I have seen it.
"Jālinīprabha, you should know this!"

Brahmā Viśeṣacintin was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who pose correct questions; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who skillfully discern all dharmas; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who explain the intended meaning of the sūtras according to what is appropriate; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas with a mind of loving-kindness; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas with a mind of compassion; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas with a mind of sympathetic joy; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas with a mind of equanimity; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who speak with gentle words; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who are free from anger and obstruction; he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who first inquire after others' welfare; and he was the foremost among all bodhisattvas who resolve doubts.

At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, prostrated their heads at the feet of the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“The World-Honored One of great renown Is universally heard throughout the ten directions;
Among all the Tathāgatas wherever they may be, There are none who do not offer praise.”
There are other pure lands where even the names of the three evil realms do not exist;
having relinquished such wondrous lands, you were born here out of compassion.
Your Buddha-wisdom is no less than that of all Tathāgatas.
By virtue of his great compassion and original vow, he dwells in this defiled and evil land.
If a person were to maintain the precepts in a pure land for an entire kalpa,
practicing compassion in this land for even a brief moment would be far superior.
If a person in this land commits offenses of body, speech,
or mind that would cause them to fall into the three evil realms, they shall receive purification in this very life.
Bodhisattvas born in this land should not harbor anxiety or fear.
Should there be the karmic offenses of the evil realms, the headache shall be immediately relieved.
If the bodhisattvas of this land can protect the Dharma,
in every place where they are born throughout their successive lives, they shall not lose right mindfulness.
If a person wishes to sever their bonds, extinguish the karmic offenses of afflictions,
protect the Dharma in this land, and increase all-encompassing wisdom, they should,
for many billions of kalpas in the Pure Land, uphold and explain this Dharma.
In this Sahā world, from dawn until the time of the meal,
I have seen the Land of Joy and the Land of Peace;
herein there is no suffering or affliction, nor even the name of such things.
To perform meritorious deeds there is not yet to be considered marvelous;
but to be able to endure what is unbearable here in this realm of afflictions,
and to teach this Dharma to others as well— that merit is the most supreme.
I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate Savior from Suffering,
who is able to preach the Dharma for the sake of evil sentient beings— a task most difficult to perform.
The Buddha has gathered immeasurable multitudes from throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The Bodhisattvas of Renown from all directions listen to the Dharma without ever being satiated.
The Buddha gathers the Bodhisattvas of Renown from the worlds of the ten directions;
they listen to the Dharma without ever being satiated, like the ocean swallowing all streams.
For the sake of such persons as these, he extensively expounds the Buddha-way;
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and all the devas, nāgas, and spirits have gathered,
desiring to seek the Dharma, so that he may preach according to their respective inclinations and joys.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as laymen and laywomen of pure faith—
may you now expound the teaching for this assembly of the four groups who delight in the Buddha-vehicle,
as well as those of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.
The Buddha, knowing their profound intentions, has completely severed all doubts for them.
Those who do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas are able to give birth to the Triple Gem;
for the sake of these bodhisattvas, I now entreat the Dharma King.
His fame spreads everywhere; Bodhisattvas from the ten directions hear it and all gather together, for he shall preach the Unsurpassed Way.
This unsurpassed Great Dharma is beyond the reach of the two vehicles.
By the power of our faith, we have been able to enter into such a Dharma;
this inconceivable wisdom is beyond our reach.
Although the Buddha is free from weariness, we nevertheless make this request.
"I repent before the World-Honored One; may you please explain the path to bodhi.
Chapter Two: The Four Dharmas (1) At that time, after the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose mind is firm and free from weariness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose words are definitive and not subject to regret?
What is meant by a bodhisattva increasing their roots of goodness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being fearless and having unshakable deportment?
What is meant by a bodhisattva accomplishing the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*)?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully knowing how to proceed from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of expedient means among sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful transformation of sentient beings?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not losing the mind of enlightenment from lifetime to lifetime?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to unify the mind and remain free from mixed conduct?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully seeking the treasure of the Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully emerging from the transgression of violating the precepts?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful obscuring of afflictions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful entry into great assemblies?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful opening of the gift of Dharma?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the power of prior causes so as not to lose their roots of goodness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice the six pāramitās through their own initiative, without relying on the instruction of others?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to relinquish meditative concentration and return to birth in the desire realm?
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not severing the lineage of the Buddhas?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Brahmā Viśeṣacintin:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a matter."
"Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well!
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy."
The Buddha told Brahmā Viśeṣacintin:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva fortifies their mind and remains free from weariness.
What are these four?"
First, to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;
second, to be diligent and untiring;
third, to believe and understand that birth and death are like a dream.
"Fourth, they correctly contemplate the wisdom of the Buddha.
When a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, they fortify their mind and do not grow weary. O Brahmā!"
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which what they say is definitive and free from subsequent regret.
What are these four?
First, they definitively teach that all phenomena are without self.
Second, they resolutely teach that no place of birth is to be desired;
third, they resolutely and constantly praise the Mahāyāna;
fourth, they resolutely teach that the karma of transgressions and merits is never lost.
These are the four.
"Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva increases their roots of goodness."
What are the four?
First, upholding the precepts;
second, extensive learning.
Third is giving; fourth is renouncing the household life.
These are the four.
“Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is without fear and their majestic deportment remains unshakable.
What are these four?
First, loss of profit;
second, ill repute; third, humiliation.
The fourth is suffering and affliction. These are the four. "Brahmā!
A bodhisattva possesses four dharmas that bring about the accomplishment of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
What are these four?
First, teaching others to believe in transgression and merit.
Second, practicing generosity without seeking karmic retribution;
third, safeguarding the true Dharma;
and fourth, instructing all bodhisattvas with wisdom.
These are the four.
"Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully knows how to proceed from one stage to the next."
What are the four?
First, having long cultivated roots of goodness;
second, being free from all faults and transgressions.
Third, skillfully knowing the means of dedication;
fourth, practicing with diligent vigor. These are the four.
“Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully understands expedient means (upāya).
What are these four?
First, to act in accordance with the intentions of sentient beings;
second, to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the merits of others;
third, to repent and eliminate transgressions.
Fourth is to exhort and entreat all Buddhas. These are the four. "Brahmā!
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully transforms sentient beings.
What are the four?
First, constantly seeking the benefit and peace of sentient beings;
Second, relinquishing one's own pleasure;
third, mental harmony and patience;
fourth, abandoning arrogance.
"These are the four.
Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not lose the mind of awakening from lifetime to lifetime."
What are the four?
First, constantly recollecting the Buddha;
second, dedicating all performed merits toward Bodhi.
Third, associating with virtuous friends;
fourth, extolling the Mahāyāna. These are the four.
“Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can unify the mind and remain free from mixed conduct.
What are these four?
First, to be free from the mind of a śrāvaka;
second, to be free from the mind of a pratyekabuddha;
third, to seek the Dharma without weariness.
"Fourth, to extensively expound for others the Dharma as it has been heard.
These are the four. Brahmā! "
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which they skillfully seek the jewel of the Dharma.
What are these four?
First, they conceive the notion that the Dharma is a jewel because it is difficult to obtain.
Second, one should conceive of the Dharma as medicine, because it cures all ailments;
third, one should conceive of the Dharma as wealth and profit, because it is never lost;
fourth, one should conceive of the Dharma as the extinction of all suffering, because it leads to Nirvana.
These are the four.
"Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully emerges from the transgression of violating the precepts."
What are the four?
First, attaining the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because all phenomena have no coming;
second, attaining the patience of non-extinction, because all phenomena have no going.
Third, attaining the patience of causes and conditions, because one knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
fourth, attaining the patience of non-abiding, because there is no continuity of divergent mental states.
These are the four.
"Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva effectively obstructs the afflictions."
What are the four?
First, right mindfulness;
second, restraining the sense faculties.
Third, attaining the power of wholesome dharmas;
fourth, dwelling alone in seclusion.
These are the four.
“Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully enters among the great assemblies.
What are these four?
First, seeking the Dharma, not seeking victory;
second, being respectful, with a mind free from arrogance;
third, seeking only the benefit of the Dharma, without self-display.
Fourth, teaching others the wholesome Dharma without seeking fame or profit.
These are the four. "Brahmā!
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which they skillfully open the gift of Dharma.
What are these four?
First, they guard and protect the Dharma.
Second, to benefit one's own wisdom and also that of others;
third, to practice the dharmas of virtuous persons;
fourth, to demonstrate to others defilement and purity.
These are the four. "Brahmā!
There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the power of prior causes and does not lose their roots of goodness. What are these four?
First, not regarding the deficiencies of others as faults;
second, constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness toward those who are angry;
third, always explaining the causes and conditions of all phenomena.
The fourth is to constantly keep awakening in mind. These are the four. "Brahmā!
Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which they are able to practice the six pāramitās on their own, without being taught by others.
What are these four?
First, they lead others by means of giving.
Second, not speaking of the transgressions of others who have violated the precepts;
third, skillfully knowing the methods of gathering [disciples] and teaching and transforming sentient beings;
fourth, understanding and penetrating the profound Dharma.
These are the four.
"Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is able to relinquish meditative concentration and be reborn again in the desire realm."
What are the four? First, his mind is supple;
second, he attains the power of the faculties.
Third, not abandoning any sentient being;
fourth, skillfully cultivating the power of wisdom and expedient means.
These are the four.
“Brahmā! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
What are the four?
First, undergoing immeasurable births and deaths;
second, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
third, practicing immeasurable loving-kindness.
Fourth, to have faith and understanding in the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas.
These are the four. "Brahmā!
Bodhisattvas possess four dharmas by which they do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
What are these four?
First, they do not retreat from their original vows.
Second, one's words must be put into practice;
third, one possesses great aspiration and diligence;
fourth, one practices the Buddha-way with a profound mind.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
When these four dharmas were spoken, twenty-two thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and five thousand people attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*).
The bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions made offerings to the Buddha; the celestial flowers they scattered filled the entire trichiliocosm, accumulating up to the knees.

Brahmā replied:
“World-Honored One!
If a dharma is illusory, that dharma should neither be said to exist nor should it be said not to exist. “What do you think?”
"If a dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, can that dharma be attained?
Brahmā replied, "There is no one who attains it."
“Brahmā! When the Tathāgata sat at the site of enlightenment, he realized only the ultimate emptiness of the afflictions arising from false and inverted perceptions.
He attained it through non-attainment; he knew it through non-knowing.”

Why is this? The Dharma I have realized cannot be seen, cannot be heard, cannot be sensed, and cannot be cognized; it cannot be grasped and cannot be clung to; it cannot be spoken and cannot be contested.
It transcends all characteristics of dharmas; it is without speech, without discourse, without letters, and without the path of verbal expression.
Brahmā! This Dharma is thus, just like space.
Do you wish to gain benefit within such a Dharma?
Brahmā said: “No, World-Honored One.”

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are most rare and marvelous; they have accomplished unprecedented dharmas, have deeply entered great loving-kindness and great compassion, and having attained such a dharma of the mark of cessation, they teach others by means of words and letters so that they may attain it as well.
“World-Honored One!
Those who, upon hearing this, are able to believe and understand it—know that such persons have not come from small merit.
World-Honored One!”
This Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe. Why is this?
Because the world clings to reality, yet this Dharma is neither real nor illusory.
The world is attached to dharmas, yet these dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas;
the world is attached to nirvāṇa, yet these dharmas have neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
the world is attached to wholesome dharmas, yet these dharmas are neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
The world is attached to pleasure, yet this Dharma is neither suffering nor pleasure;
the world is attached to the appearance of a Buddha in the world, yet this Dharma has neither the appearance of a Buddha nor Nirvana;
although there is the preaching of the Dharma, this Dharma is not of a nature that can be expressed in words.
Although one praises and speaks of the Sangha, the Sangha is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, this Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe.
It is, for example, like fire emerging from water or water emerging from fire; it is difficult to find anyone who can believe it.
That within these afflictions there is bodhi, and within bodhi there are afflictions—this too is difficult to believe. Why is this?

It is because the Tathāgata has realized the nature of these illusory afflictions, yet there is no dharma he does not attain; though he teaches the Dharma, it has no form; though he possesses knowledge, there is no discrimination; and though he realizes nirvāṇa, there is nothing that ceases.
“World-Honored One!
If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to believe in and understand the meaning of such Dharma,
you should know that these persons have attained liberation from all views.”
One should know that this person has already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas;
one should know that this person has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
one should know that this person is protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
One should know that this person’s resolve is vast and expansive;
one should know that this person’s roots of goodness are profound and deep;
one should know that this person protects the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
One should know that such a person is capable of skillful deliberation and gives rise to wholesome karma;
one should know that such a person is of noble lineage and is born into the family of the Tathāgata;
one should know that such a person is able to practice great relinquishment and abandon all afflictions.
One should know that such a person attains the power of ethical discipline, not the power of afflictions;
one should know that such a person attains the power of patience, not the power of anger;
one should know that such a person attains the power of diligence, free from weariness and indolence.
It should be known that such a person attains the power of meditative concentration and extinguishes all evil thoughts;
it should be known that such a person attains the power of wisdom and is free from evil and false views;
it should be known that all evil Māras cannot find an opportunity against them.
One should know that such a person cannot be defeated by any enemies or thieves;
one should know that such a person does not deceive the world;
one should know that such a person is a speaker of truth, for they skillfully explain the characteristics of dharmas.
One should know that this person is a speaker of truth, because they speak of the ultimate meaning;
one should know that this person is well-protected and remembered by all Buddhas;
one should know that this person is gentle, mild, and virtuous, and that dwelling together with them is peaceful and happy.
One should know that such a person is called "greatly wealthy," because they possess the noble riches;
one should know that such a person is always able to be content, because they practice the noble lineages;
one should know that such a person is easy to satisfy and easy to support, because they are free from greedy attachment.
One should know that such a person attains a mind of peace and security because they have reached the other shore;
one should know that such a person delivers those who have not yet been delivered;
one should know that such a person liberates those who have not yet been liberated.
One should know that such a person brings peace to those who have not yet found peace;
one should know that such a person extinguishes what has not yet been extinguished;
one should know that such a person is able to show the right path.
One should know that such a person is able to explain liberation;
one should know that such a person is a great king of physicians, well-versed in all medicines;
one should know that such a person is like an excellent medicine, skillfully healing all ailments.
One should know that this person’s wisdom is courageous and robust;
one should know that this person possesses great power, which is firm and ultimate;
one should know that this person has the power of diligence and does not follow the words of others.
One should know that such a person is like a lion, possessing no fear;
one should know that such a person is like a king of elephants, their mind being well-tamed and gentle;
one should know that such a person is like an aged elephant, their mind being compliant and harmonious.
One should know that such a person is like a bull-king, able to lead the great assembly;
one should know that such a person is of great courage and prowess, able to shatter the enmity of Māra;
one should know that such a person is a true mahāsattva, dwelling among the multitude without fear.
One should know that this person has nothing to fear or hesitate about, for they have attained the dharma of fearlessness;
one should know that this person has no dread or difficulty, for they proclaim the dharma of ultimate truth;
one should know that this person is endowed with pure and white dharmas, like the full moon.
One should know that this person’s light of wisdom shines like the brilliance of the sun;
one should know that this person dispels all darkness like one who holds a torch;
one should know that this person delights in practicing equanimity, remaining free from all hatred and attachment.
One should know that such a person sustains and nurtures sentient beings, just like the earth;
one should know that such a person washes away all defilements and dust, just like water;
one should know that such a person burns away all restless thoughts, just like fire.
One should know that such a person is unimpeded regarding the Dharma, like the wind;
one should know that their mind is immovable, like Mount Sumeru;
one should know that their mind is firm and solid, like a diamond mountain.
One should know that such a person cannot be moved by any of the proponents of competitive doctrines among the various non-Buddhists;
one should know that such a person cannot be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
one should know that such a person abounds in the treasures of the Dharma, like the great ocean.
One should know that this person’s afflictions do not manifest, like the pāṭala flower;
one should know that this person seeks the Dharma without weariness;
one should know that this person is content through wisdom.
One should know that such a person is able to turn the wheel of Dharma, like a wheel-turning monarch;
one should know that the physical form and color of such a person are exceptionally sublime, like Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
one should know that the mind of such a person has attained mastery, like Brahmā, King of the Gods.
One should know that the sound of this person’s preaching of the Dharma is like the roar of thunder;
one should know that this person bestows the nectar of the Dharma, like seasonal rain;
one should know that this person is able to increase the untainted faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment.
One should know that such a person has already crossed over the mire of birth and death;
one should know that such a person has entered the wisdom of the Buddha;
one should know that such a person is close to the Bodhi of the Buddha.
One should know that this person is able to study extensively such that none can equal them;
one should know that this person is immeasurable and has already transcended all measure;
one should know that this person’s wisdom and eloquence are free from all obstruction.
It should be known that this person attains firm mindfulness and acquires dhāraṇī;
it should be known that this person knows the deep mental activities of all sentient beings;
it should be known that this person attains the power of wisdom, correctly contemplates all phenomena, and thoroughly understands their underlying meanings.
One should know that such a person practices with diligent vigor for the benefit and peace of the world;
one should know that such a person transcends the world;
one should know that such a person cannot be defiled, just like a lotus flower.
One should know that such a person is not obscured by worldly dharmas;
one should know that such a person is beloved by those of sharp faculties;
one should know that such a person is revered by those of great learning.
One should know that such a person is cherished by the wise;
one should know that such a person is honored by humans and devas;
one should know that such a person is revered and saluted by those who practice dhyāna.
One should know that such a person is esteemed by the virtuous;
one should know that such a person is coveted and admired by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
one should know that such a person does not crave minor practices.
One should know that this person does not conceal their faults nor boast of their virtues;
one should know that this person is fully endowed with dignified deportment, giving rise to pure faith in others;
one should know that this person’s physical form is upright and handsome, bringing joy and delight to all who behold them.
One should know that this person possesses great majestic power and is revered by all;
one should know that this person adorns their body with the thirty-two marks;
one should know that this person is able to continue the lineage of the Buddhas.
One should know that such a person is able to protect the treasure of the Dharma;
one should know that such a person is able to make offerings to the Saṃgha;
one should know that such a person is beheld by all Buddhas.
One should know that such a person has attained the Dharma-eye;
one should know that such a person has received the prediction of enlightenment through the Buddha’s wisdom;
one should know that such a person is fully endowed with the three kinds of patience.
One should know that such a person dwells securely in the site of enlightenment;
one should know that such a person destroys the armies of Māra;
one should know that such a person attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
It should be known that such a person turns the wheel of Dharma;
it should be known that such a person performs immeasurable Buddha-works.

"If a person believes and understands the meaning of such Dharma, and is not startled, doubtful, or terrified, they shall obtain such merit—namely, that regarding the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, which is profoundly deep, difficult to understand, difficult to know, difficult to believe, and difficult to enter, they are able to believe and accept it, read and recite it, master it, uphold it, explain it extensively for others, practice according to its teaching, and also instruct others to practice according to its teaching."
"For such a person as this, even if I were to spend an eon, or slightly less than an eon, speaking of their merits, I could not exhaustively describe them.

The remainder of Chapter Four, “Explanation of All Dharmas”; Chapter Six, “The Exposition of the Five Powers of the Tathāgata. Fifth scroll. The World-Honored One said: “What is called Great Compassion? Below is Chapter Seven, “The Tathāgata’s Great Compassion. The Buddha addressed Brahmā:
"How could you possibly describe the merits of this person?
Those merits exceed even what the Tathāgata knows through his unimpeded wisdom."

If a person can thoroughly penetrate and accord with the letters, speech, and phrases spoken by the Tathāgata—neither opposing nor contradicting them, but harmonizing them into a unity—and follow their underlying principles rather than merely following the literal words and phrases, thereby skillfully knowing the characteristics appropriate to those words;

and knows by what language the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, by what suitability he preaches the Dharma, by what skillful means he preaches the Dharma, by what Dharma-gates he preaches the Dharma, and by what great compassion he preaches the Dharma.
"Brahmā! If a bodhisattva can know that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of these five powers, that bodhisattva is able to perform the work of a Buddha. Brahmā said:
“What are the five powers employed by the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said: “The first is speech.”
Second, acting according to what is appropriate;
third, skillful means;
fourth, Dharma gates.
"Fifth is great compassion.
These are called the five powers employed by the Tathāgata, which no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can equal.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
"What is meant by 'expounding the Dharma'? The Buddha said, "Brahmā!

The Tathāgata speaks of past dharmas, speaks of future and present dharmas; he speaks of defiled and pure dharmas; he speaks of mundane and supramundane dharmas; he speaks of dharmas with fault and dharmas without fault; he speaks of dharmas with outflows and dharmas without outflows; he speaks of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; he speaks of dharmas regarding the self, the person, sentient beings, and the life-span; he speaks of dharmas of realization and attainment; and he speaks of dharmas of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
Brahmā! You should know that all these verbal expressions are like the speech of a phantom person, for they lack any fixed reality;
they are like speech within a dream, for they are seen as false and illusory.
It is said to be like an echo, because it issues from emptiness;
it is said to be like a shadow, because it arises from the conjunction of various conditions;
it is said to be like a reflection in a mirror, because the cause does not enter the mirror.
It is said to be like a mirage because of inverted views;
it is said to be like space because it is without arising or ceasing.
One should know that this teaching is a teaching of nothing taught, for the characteristics of all dharmas are ineffable.
Brahmā! If a bodhisattva can understand these various teachings, then although there are all manner of verbal expressions, they will have no attachment to any phenomena;
because they are without attachment, they attain unimpeded eloquence.

By means of this eloquence, one may preach the Dharma for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges without exhaustion or obstruction; all such verbal expressions do not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), nor do they cling to or destroy the nature of phenomena.
"Brahmā! This is what the Tathāgata calls teaching. Brahmā said:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘according to what is appropriate’? The Buddha said:
“The Tathāgata may describe defiled phenomena as pure, or pure phenomena as defiled.
In this regard, a bodhisattva should understand that these are the Tathāgata’s teachings given according to what is appropriate. Brahmā!
What is meant by describing defiled phenomena as pure?
Because the intrinsic nature of defiled phenomena cannot be apprehended.
What is meant by describing pure phenomena as defiled?
Because they are greedily attached to pure phenomena.
Furthermore, Brahmā!
I say that giving itself is nirvāṇa; yet ordinary people, lacking wisdom, are unable to properly understand what has been taught according to their needs.
A bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"After practicing giving, one obtains great wealth; yet herein, no dharma can be apprehended.

From one moment of thought to the next—if there were no transition from one moment of thought to the next, that would be the true mark of all dharmas (dharmatā); and the true mark of all dharmas is nirvāṇa."
“Observing the precepts is nirvana, because there is no acting and no arising;
patience is nirvana, because every thought-moment ceases;
diligence is nirvana, because there is nothing to be grasped.”
Dhyāna-concentration is nirvāṇa, because it does not crave its flavor;
wisdom is nirvāṇa, because it does not apprehend signs;
craving is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without desire.
Hatred is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without hatred;
delusion is the limit of reality, because the nature of phenomena is without delusion;
birth-and-death is *nirvāṇa*, because there is neither retrogression nor arising.
Nirvāṇa is saṃsāra because of attachment;
true speech is false because it gives rise to views regarding speech;
and falsehood is true speech for the sake of those with overweening pride.
"Furthermore, Brahmā!
Because the Tathāgata acts according to what is appropriate, he may sometimes speak of a self, which is a teaching regarding the extreme of eternalism;
or he may sometimes speak of a self, which is a teaching regarding the extreme of annihilationism."
Some speak of a self while asserting that there is no agent;
some speak of a self while holding wrong views;
some speak of a self while lacking faith.
Some declare of themselves, "I am one who does not know how to repay kindness";
some declare of themselves, "I am one who eats vomit";
some declare of themselves, "I am one who does not receive."

The Tathāgata does not possess such things; one should know that these are spoken according to what is appropriate, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to abandon their overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

If a bodhisattva thoroughly understands the Tathāgata’s skillful means in teaching, they will, upon hearing that a Buddha has appeared, believe and accept it, because [the Buddha] manifests to sentient beings the physical body (*rūpakāya*) as the fruit of wholesome karma;
and they will, upon hearing that a Buddha has not appeared, likewise believe and accept it, knowing that this is the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) of all Buddhas.
If they hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, they believe and accept it, for the sake of sentient beings who delight in words and letters;
if they hear the Buddha not preach the Dharma, they also believe and accept it, knowing that the nature of the positions of all dharmas is ineffable;
if they hear that there is nirvana, they also believe and accept it, because it extinguishes the afflictions arising from perversion.
If one hears that there is no nirvana, one accepts it with faith because all phenomena lack the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
if one hears that there are sentient beings, one accepts it with faith because one has entered the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
if one hears that there are no sentient beings, one accepts it with faith because one has entered the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Brahmā! Thus, the bodhisattva skillfully understands the Tathāgata’s teachings as expressed according to what is appropriate; they are without doubt or fear regarding any sounds, and are likewise able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘expedient means’ (upāya)? The Buddha said:

“The Tathāgata teaches sentient beings that by practicing generosity one attains great wealth; by observing the precepts one attains rebirth in the heavens; by practicing patience one attains physical beauty; by practicing diligence one becomes endowed with all merits; by practicing meditative concentration one attains the joy of the Dharma; by practicing wisdom one attains the relinquishing of all afflictions; by possessing extensive learning one attains wisdom; by practicing the ten paths of wholesome action one attains the blissful fortune of humans and devas; by practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity one attains rebirth in the Brahma world; by practicing meditative concentration one attains wisdom according to reality; by attaining wisdom according to reality one attains the fruits of the Path; by training on the stage of learning one attains the stage of no-more-learning; by attaining the stage of the Pratyekabuddha one attains the digestion of all offerings; by attaining the stage of Buddhahood one attains immeasurable wisdom; and by attaining Nirvāṇa one attains the extinction of all suffering and affliction.”
Brahmā! It is by such skillful means that I praise and teach this Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

In reality, the Tathāgata does not apprehend a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; nor does he apprehend giving, nor does he apprehend stinginess; nor does he apprehend precepts, nor does he apprehend the breaking of precepts; nor does he apprehend patience, nor does he apprehend anger; nor does he apprehend diligence, nor does he apprehend indolence; nor does he apprehend meditative concentration, nor does he apprehend a distracted mind; nor does he apprehend wisdom, nor does he apprehend the fruit of wisdom; nor does he apprehend bodhi, nor does he apprehend nirvāṇa; nor does he apprehend suffering, nor does he apprehend pleasure.
Brahmā! If sentient beings hear this Dharma and practice with diligent vigor, for what benefit would such persons practice with diligent vigor and yet fail to attain this Dharma?
Furthermore, one cannot obtain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the path of pratyekabuddha, anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, or even nirvāṇa.
"Brahmā! This is called the Tathāgata’s skillful means of teaching the Dharma.
Within this skillful means of teaching the Dharma, a bodhisattva should apply diligent effort so that all sentient beings may obtain the benefits of the Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
What is called the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
"The eye is a gate of liberation; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are gates of liberation.
Why is this? The eye is empty, selfless, and devoid of what belongs to a self; such is its very nature."
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these are empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self; such is their inherent nature.
Brahmā! You should know that all sense bases enter this gate of liberation, for when one practices correctly, there is no falsehood.
Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are likewise so;

all dharmas enter this gate, namely: the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, the gate of wishlessness, the gate of non-arising, the gate of non-ceasing, the gate of having no place from which they come, the gate of having no place to which they go, the gate of non-retrogression, the gate of non-origination, the gate of the eternally pure nature, and the gate of being devoid of self-substance.
Furthermore, Brahmā!
The Tathāgata reveals this gate of liberation within all written characters. Why is this so?
All syllables are neither combined nor functional, for their nature is dull. Brahmā!

You should know that within all syllables, the Tathāgata speaks of the Noble Truths and speaks of the gates of liberation. The Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is without defilement; all phenomena enter into liberation and cause them to abide in nirvāṇa. This is called the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma entering the Dharma-gate.
“A bodhisattva should train in this Dharma-gate.
“World-Honored One,
what is called ‘great compassion’?”
The Buddha said:
“The Tathāgata protects and delivers sentient beings through thirty-two kinds of great compassion.
What are these thirty-two? ”
All phenomena are without self, yet sentient beings do not believe or understand this, asserting instead that there is a self that is born;
it is regarding this that the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are without sentient beings, yet sentient beings assert that there are sentient beings.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this:
although all dharmas are devoid of a life-span, sentient beings claim that there is a life-span;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this.
All phenomena are devoid of a person, yet sentient beings speak of there being a person;
regarding this, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are non-existent, yet sentient beings abide in the view of existence.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this:
while all dharmas are without abiding, sentient beings abide;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this.
All phenomena have no place of refuge, yet sentient beings delight in places of refuge;
for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are not "mine," yet sentient beings are attached to what is "mine"; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this:
all dharmas have no ownership, yet sentient beings conceive of there being ownership;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this.
All phenomena are without the characteristic of grasping, yet sentient beings grasp at characteristics;
for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are without arising, yet sentient beings abide in the state of arising; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this:
all phenomena are free from retrogression and rebirth, yet sentient beings abide in retrogression and rebirth;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this.
All phenomena are stainless, yet sentient beings cling to defilement;
for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are free from passion, yet sentient beings possess passion; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this:
all dharmas are free from hatred, yet sentient beings harbor hatred;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this.
All dharmas are free from delusion, yet sentient beings possess delusion;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this.
All dharmas come from nowhere, yet sentient beings cling to the notion that they come from somewhere.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this:
all phenomena have no place of departure, yet sentient beings are attached to the notion of departure;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion regarding this.
All dharmas are without arising, yet sentient beings conceive of there being arising;
for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All dharmas are without conceptual proliferation, yet sentient beings are attached to conceptual proliferation; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this:
although all phenomena are empty, sentient beings fall into the view of existence;
the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this.
All dharmas are signless, yet sentient beings cling to signs;
for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
All dharmas are without action, yet sentient beings cling to action; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this:
that the world is constantly engaged in anger, resentment, and contention; the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this:
that the world, with its wrong views and inverted perceptions, wanders upon the path of error.
Desiring to cause them to abide in the Right Path, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this.
The world is gluttonous and never satisfied, mutually encroaching upon and seizing one another;
desiring to cause sentient beings to abide in the noble wealth—faith, precepts, learning, generosity, wisdom, and so forth—the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for this.
Sentient beings are slaves to their wealth, wives, children, and attachments, conceiving notions of solidity toward these fragile things;
wishing to cause sentient beings to fully realize impermanence, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them.
Sentient beings take their own bodies as enemies and thieves, yet they are greedily attached to nourishing them as if they were dear friends;
wishing to act as true spiritual friends for sentient beings, leading them to exhaust all suffering and reach ultimate nirvana, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion herein.
Sentient beings delight in practicing deception and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood;

wishing to cause them to practice right livelihood, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them. Sentient beings take pleasure in and are attached to the household life, which is full of suffering and impurity; [wishing to cause them to renounce it, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion].
Desiring to cause them to emerge from the triple world, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion herein.
All dharmas arise from causes and conditions, yet sentient beings give rise to indolence regarding the noble liberation;
desiring to preach diligence so that they may delight in liberation, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion herein.
Sentient beings abandon the supreme, unimpeded wisdom and seek instead the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
desiring to guide them so that they may resolve upon the Great Mind and take refuge in the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for them.
Brahmā! In this way, the Tathāgata practices these thirty-two kinds of great compassion toward all sentient beings; therefore, the Tathāgata is called one who practices great compassion.

If a bodhisattva is able to constantly cultivate and accumulate this mind of great compassion among sentient beings, they will enter the stage of *avaivartika*, become a great field of merit endowed with majestic virtue, and be able to constantly benefit all sentient beings.

When this "Chapter on the Dharma-Door of Great Compassion" was being spoken, thirty-two thousand people all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
