When that Buddha approached the Bodhi tree, all the Māras and the subjects of Māra within the kingdom were established in right concentration regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

That buddha-field has the precious *saptaparṇa* sandalwood as its ground; the earth is level as the palm of a hand, soft, supple, and smooth like *kāliṅga* cloth. It is adorned everywhere with various jewels, and there are no three evil realms nor eight difficulties.
That land was vast and expansive, adorned throughout with exquisite jewel lotuses of wondrous color and fragrance.

The Tathāgata Universal Radiance Sovereign King had an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas who had skillfully cultivated immeasurable dharma-gates and attained immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers;
all of them adorned their bodies with radiance, had mastered the treasury of dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, and were well able to preach the Dharma.
He has attained complete mastery over the spiritual power of radiance and is able to destroy the enmity of Māra;
he cultivates his mind with shame, remorse, mindfulness, wisdom, and all manner of sublime virtues.

In that Buddha-land there are no women; all those bodhisattvas are born by spontaneous transformation within precious lotus flowers, sitting cross-legged, taking the bliss of dhyāna as their sustenance.
"Whatever things are required—places for walking meditation, dwellings, couches, gardens, and bathing pools—shall arrive as soon as they are thought of. Kāśyapa!..."

This Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-vibhutva-rāja does not preach the Dharma by means of words and letters; rather, he merely emits radiance that illuminates all bodhisattvas. When the light touches their bodies, they immediately attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, the Buddha’s radiance shines throughout the ten directions, penetrating everywhere without obstruction, causing all sentient beings to become free from afflictions.
Furthermore, from that radiance, thirty-two kinds of pure Dharma-sounds constantly emerge.
What are these thirty-two? They are as follows:
all phenomena are empty, because there is no perception of a sentient being.
All phenomena are signless, because they are free from conceptual discrimination.
All phenomena are unconditioned, because they transcend the triple world.
All phenomena are free from desire, because their nature is quiescent extinction.
All dharmas are free from hatred, for they are without obstruction.
All dharmas are free from delusion, for they are without darkness.
All dharmas come from nowhere, for they are fundamentally unarisen.
All phenomena have nowhere to go, for they do not arrive anywhere.
All phenomena do not abide, for they have nothing upon which to rely.
All phenomena transcend the three periods of time, for the past, future, and present are non-existent.
All phenomena are without distinction, for their nature is one.
All phenomena are unarisen, for they are free from retribution.
All phenomena are without karma, for an agent, karma, and its retribution cannot be apprehended.
All phenomena are uncreated, for they do not arise.
All phenomena are without arising, for their nature is unconditioned.
All phenomena are unconditioned, for they are free from birth and cessation.
All phenomena are true, for they do not arise from combination.
All phenomena are real, for they are the gateway to the One Path.
All phenomena are without sentient beings, for sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
All phenomena are selfless, because they are the ultimate truth.
All phenomena are insentient, because they possess no cognition.
All phenomena are equanimous, because they are free from hatred and attachment.
All phenomena are free from afflictions, for they are without feverish distress.
All phenomena are stainless, for their nature is undefiled.
All phenomena have a single characteristic, for they are the limit of detachment from desire.
All phenomena are devoid of marks, for they are eternally settled.
All phenomena abide in the limit of reality, for their nature is indestructible.
All phenomena are like the suchness of reality, for they are non-discriminative.
All dharmas enter the dharma-nature because they pervasively enter it.
All dharmas are without conditions because conditions do not conjoin with them.
All dharmas are bodhi because they are seen as they truly are.
"All dharmas are nirvāṇa, because they are without causes and conditions. Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-viśeṣa-rāja constantly emits such pure sounds of the Dharma from his radiance, which enables all bodhisattvas to perform the work of Buddhas."
"In that Buddha-land there shall be no demonic interference, and the Buddha’s lifespan shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If anyone wishes to attain a pure Buddha-land, they should adopt the merits cultivated by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha to fully perfect a pure land."
“In this way, Kāśyapa, it is because this Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha has fulfilled his merit by practicing in accordance with his vows under immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas.”
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin said to the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha:
"Virtuous One, you have already received a prophecy from the Buddha.
Jālinīprabha replied:
"All sentient beings have received predictions of enlightenment from the Buddha. Brahmā asked,
"In what matters do they receive these predictions?"
Jālinīprabha said:
"One receives the prediction according to the retribution one undergoes for one's karma. Brahmā said:
“What kind of karma did you perform to receive this prediction?
Jālinīprabha replied,
“If there is karma that is not performed by body, not performed by speech, and not performed by mind, can such karma be demonstrated?”
Brahmā said, "It cannot be shown. Jālinīprabha said:
“Is awakening characterized by activity? Brahmā replied, “No.”
"Why is this? Because Bodhi is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and does not possess the characteristics of arising or activity.
Jālinīprabha said:
"Can one attain unconditioned bodhi by means of the characteristic of active effort? Brahmā replied, "No."
“Brahmā! Therefore, you should know that if there is no karma and no retribution for karma, no conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) and no arising of conditioned phenomena, this is called bodhi;
as is the nature of bodhi, so too is its attainment.”
"Just as with the attainment of the nature [of reality], so it is with receiving the prediction; one cannot receive the prediction through the performance of conditioned acts.
Brahmā said: "Good son!..."
"Is it that you will not receive the prediction of enlightenment until you have practiced the six pāramitās?
Jālinīprabha replied, "As you have said,
a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment by practicing the six pāramitās."
"Brahmā! If a bodhisattva relinquishes all afflictions, it is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
To have no arising with respect to any phenomena is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
To be unharmed by any phenomena is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
To be free from the marks of all phenomena is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To have no dwelling in any phenomena is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
To have no conceptual proliferation regarding any phenomena is called the prajñā-pāramitā. Brahmā!
When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās in this way, in what place do they practice?
Brahmā replied, "They practice in no place."
Why is this? For all that is conditioned activity is non-activity;
if there is activity, it is non-activity, and if there is no activity, it is activity.
“Brahmā! For this reason, you should know that non-practice is bodhi.
As you have asked:”
"Regarding 'you have received the prediction of enlightenment,' it is by means of suchness and the dharma-nature that one receives the prediction;
my own receipt of the prediction is likewise. Brahmā said: "Good son!..."
"Just as suchness and the dharma-nature have no [characteristic] of receiving a prediction," Jālinīprabha said,
"so too are the characteristics of the predictions received by all bodhisattvas; they are suchness and the dharma-nature."
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what practices do the Buddhas bestow the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon bodhisattvas?"
The Buddha said:
“If a bodhisattva does not practice the dharma of arising, does not practice the dharma of cessation;
does not practice what is wholesome, does not practice what is unwholesome; does not practice the mundane, does not practice the supramundane; does not practice dharmas with fault...”
He does not practice the dharma of non-offense; he does not practice tainted dharmas, nor does he practice untainted dharmas;
he does not practice conditioned dharmas, nor does he practice unconditioned dharmas; he does not practice the path of cultivation, nor does he practice abandonment;
he does not practice saṃsāra, nor does he practice nirvāṇa; he does not practice the dharma of seeing, nor does he practice the dharma of hearing.
One does not practice the dharma of awakening, nor does one practice the dharma of knowledge;
one does not practice giving, nor renunciation, nor precepts, nor concealment, nor patience, nor goodness, nor arousal,
nor diligence, nor meditation, nor samādhi, nor wisdom, nor practice.
There is no practice of knowing and no practice of attaining. Brahmā!
If a bodhisattva practices in this way, the Buddhas will bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this so? All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) involve the grasping of signs;
that which is signless and non-conceptual is bodhi.
All have that which they affirm;
that which has no affirmation is bodhi.
All conditioned activities are conceptualization.
Non-discrimination is bodhi.
All conditioned activities are fabrications;
the absence of fabrication is bodhi.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are conceptual proliferation (prapañca);
the absence of conceptual proliferation is awakening (bodhi).
Therefore, you should know that if a bodhisattva transcends all conditioned phenomena, they shall receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
“Yes, World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of ‘receiving a prediction’?
The Buddha said:

"To be free from the two marks of all phenomena is the meaning of receiving the prediction; not to discriminate between the paths of arising and ceasing is the meaning of receiving the prediction; to be free from the marks of bodily, verbal, and mental karma is the meaning of receiving the prediction."

"Brahmā! I recall that in the past there was an eon named Priyadarśana; during this eon, I made offerings to seventy-two nayutas of Buddhas, yet none of those Tathāgatas conferred a prediction of enlightenment upon me."

After another kalpa had passed, named Good Transformation, I made offerings to twenty-two billion Buddhas during this kalpa; yet these Tathāgatas also did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment.
After another kalpa had passed, named Brahmastava, I made offerings to eighteen thousand Buddhas during this kalpa; yet these Tathāgatas likewise did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment.

Furthermore, after this kalpa, there was a kalpa named "Faultless" (Anavadya); during this kalpa, I made offerings to thirty-two thousand Buddhas, yet none of these Tathāgatas granted me a prediction of enlightenment.

Furthermore, after this kalpa, there was a kalpa named Adornment; during this kalpa, I made offerings to four million four hundred thousand Buddhas, providing them with every kind of requisite for worship, yet none of these Tathāgatas granted me a prediction of enlightenment.

"Brahmā! In the past, I made offerings to all the Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them, and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring—practicing all forms of giving, all forms of ethical discipline, and the dhūtas; remaining free from anger, practicing patience and a compassionate heart; exerting diligence in accordance with what was taught; being able to receive and uphold everything I heard; dwelling alone in seclusion to enter various meditative concentrations; and reciting, contemplating, and inquiring according to the wisdom I had heard. Yet, none of those Tathāgatas granted me a prophecy."
Why is this? Because it relies upon their practice.
By this one should know that if bodhisattvas transcend all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), they shall receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
“Brahmā, were I to spend an eon, or even less than an eon, speaking these names of the Buddhas, I could not exhaust them.
Brahmā, after this,
I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and immediately attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas.”
At that time, the Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, I transcended all conditioned activities and became fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*.

Why is this? If a bodhisattva can relinquish all signs, it is called the *dāna-pāramitā*; if they can extinguish all that is grasped and maintained, it is called the *śīla-pāramitā*; if they are not harmed by the six sense objects, it is called the *kṣānti-pāramitā*; if they are detached from all conditioned practices, it is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*; if they do not give rise to recollections of any phenomena, it is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*; and if they can endure the non-arising nature of all phenomena, it is called the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I fully perfected these six pāramitās. O Brahmā!

All the gifts I have given since first generating the bodhicitta do not equal even one hundredth part of this gift of five flowers; they do not equal one ten-thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can they even be reached by calculation or analogy."

Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have received and maintained the precepts and practiced the dhūtas; yet compared to this constant extinction of the precepts, my practice does not equal even one hundredth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, my gentleness and patience have not approached even one-hundredth part of this ultimate dharma of patience; indeed, they cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.

Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have exerted diligent effort; yet this effort of neither grasping nor rejecting does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor can it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.

Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have practiced meditative concentration in solitary retreat; yet, compared to this concentration of non-abiding, my former practice does not equal even a hundredth part of it, nor can it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor.

Compared to this wisdom free from conceptual proliferation, the wisdom I have contemplated and deliberated upon since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one ten-thousandth, nor one hundred-thousandth, nor one billionth, nor even one trillionth; it is beyond all calculation and analogy.
"Brahmā! Therefore, you should know that at that time I attained the fulfillment of the six pāramitās.
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by being fully endowed with the six pāramitās? O Brahmā!

If one does not think of giving, does not rely on precepts, does not discriminate regarding patience, does not grasp at diligence, does not dwell in meditative concentration, and is non-dual regarding wisdom—this is called being fully endowed with the six pāramitās."
He asked again:
"Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, what dharma can one bring to completion?
The Buddha said:
“Having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñā.
“World-Honored One,
how is it that having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñā?”
“Brahmā! The equality of giving is itself the equality of sarvajñā;
the equality of ethical discipline is itself the equality of sarvajñā.”
The equality of patience is the equality of sarvajñā;
the equality of diligence is the equality of sarvajñā;
the equality of meditative concentration is the equality of sarvajñā.
The equality of wisdom is itself the equality of sarvajñā (all-knowledge);
by means of this equality, one equalizes all dharmas, and this is called sarvajñā.
Furthermore, Brahmā!

To be fully endowed with the marks of generosity, the marks of ethical discipline, the marks of patience, the marks of diligence, the marks of meditative concentration, and the marks of wisdom—this is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
"Brahmā! Thus, by being fully endowed with the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
"World-Honored One!"
"How should one know that all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is fulfilled?

"Brahmā! If one does not grasp at the eye, does not grasp at forms; does not grasp at the ear, does not grasp at sounds; does not grasp at the nose, does not grasp at odors; does not grasp at the tongue, does not grasp at flavors; does not grasp at the body, does not grasp at tangibles; and does not grasp at the mind, does not grasp at phenomena—if one does not grasp at these twelve internal and external bases (āyatana), this is called the fulfillment of all-knowledge."

Having attained such fulfillment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), I am unattached to the eye, and unattached to forms; likewise unattached to the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called one who possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision of omniscience.
Brahmā! Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) does not receive anything regarding phenomena. Why is this?
Because it is without utility.
To be without utility is the meaning of non-existence.

The meaning of non-existence is emptiness, which has the same meaning as space and the same characteristics as space; this is *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Therefore, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to be apprehended.
Brahmā! Just as all that is created depends upon space, yet space has nothing upon which it depends;
so too do all forms of wisdom arise from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), yet omniscience has nothing upon which it depends.
The Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the World-Honored One has spoken of as ‘sarvajñatā,’ what is meant by ‘sarvajñatā’?”
“Brahmā! All that is practiced is true wisdom; because it is not within the reach of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it is called sarvajñā (all-knowledge).”
Because all that is practiced can be brought to fulfillment, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it can shatter all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of thought, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because all the various instructions and all the various regulations, as well as the dharmas practiced by these sentient beings, all emerge from within it, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Because one attains all noble wisdoms—whether the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas—all emerge from within it, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because it is correct practice, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it can distinguish all medicines, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because it can extinguish the illnesses of all sentient beings, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Because it can eliminate all habitual tendencies of affliction, it is called sarvajña.
Because it is always in meditative concentration, it is called sarvajña.
Because it is free from doubt regarding all phenomena, it is called sarvajña.
Because all mundane and supramundane wisdoms emerge from within it, it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it skillfully knows the characteristics of all wisdom and skillful means, it is called *sarvajñā*.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha,
saying: “It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
The wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is profoundly deep; with no object of mental focus, they know the minds and mental activities of all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
Since *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) possesses such immeasurable merits, what son or daughter of good family would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) out of a desire for merit and benefit, this is not called setting forth in the Great Vehicle.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas possess no merit or benefit, as they lack any point of opposition.
World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of the benefit of merit; rather, they should resolve upon bodhicitta solely for the sake of great compassion, for the sake of extinguishing the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, for the sake of not being distressed by their own suffering, for the sake of giving rise to all wholesome dharmas, for the sake of liberating oneself from all false views, for the sake of eliminating all illnesses, for the sake of abandoning attachment to "mine," for the sake of not observing hatred or love, for the sake of not sinking into worldly dharmas, for the sake of wearying of conditioned existence, and for the sake of abiding securely in nirvāṇa.

"Bhagavān! A bodhisattva should not seek a reward of gratitude from sentient beings, nor should they observe what is done or what is left undone; furthermore, their mind should remain unmoved by suffering or pleasure."
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by the purity of a bodhisattva’s family?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva is born into the family of a universal monarch (cakravartin), this is not called purity of family;
if he is born among the Śakras or among the Brahmā kings, this likewise is not called purity of family.

In whatever place they are born, even among animals, they do not themselves lose their roots of goodness, and they also cause sentient beings to give rise to various roots of goodness; this is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s lineage.
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha!
Loving-kindness is the home of a bodhisattva, because the mind is impartial;
compassion is the home of a bodhisattva, because of the profound intention of mindfulness.
Joy is the home of the bodhisattva, because it gives rise to the joy of the Dharma;
equanimity is the home of the bodhisattva, because it is free from greedy attachment;
not abandoning bodhicitta is the home of the bodhisattva, because one does not crave the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
