Translated by Kumārajīva. Chapter Seven: Discourse (Part Three). Chapter Seven: Discourse. [In the *Dabanruoshierjing*, this corresponds to Chapter Twelve: The Non-duality of Bodhisattvas. At that time, the Brahma-heavenly being Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī is present in this great assembly, yet he says nothing.
The Buddha then addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Within the Dharma you have taught in this assembly, you may briefly explain a portion of it."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
can the Dharma attained by the Buddha be cognized?"
The Buddha said,
"It cannot be known. [He asked,] "World-Honored One!"
"Can this Dharma be spoken, expounded, or discussed?
The Buddha said,
"It cannot be spoken, it cannot be expounded, and it cannot be discussed."
“World-Honored One!
If these dharmas are unspeakable, unexpoundable, and undebatable, then they cannot be demonstrated.
At that time, Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Do you not expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā!..."
“Are there two characteristics within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)? Brahmā replied, “No.”
Mañjuśrī said: "Do all phenomena not enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?
The Brahmā replied:
"Indeed! Mañjuśrī said:
"If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-dual, and all phenomena enter into that nature of phenomena, how should one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?"
The Brahmā said: "Is there perhaps a teaching of the Dharma that is also non-dual? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If it were determined that there are both a speaker and a listener, then there would be the teaching of the Dharma, yet there would still be no duality. "Mañjuśrī!
Does the Tathāgata not teach the Dharma?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Although the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he does not do so by means of dualistic characteristics. Why is this?
"Because the nature of the Tathāgata is non-dual, although he has something to say, it is without duality. Brahmā said:
"If all dharmas are non-dual, who is it that constitutes duality?"
Mañjuśrī said: "It is because of the arising of attachment to a self that one discriminates between two;
as for the non-dual, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is ultimately not dual."
"Although various conceptual distinctions are made as 'two,' in its ultimate reality there are no two characteristics.
Brahmā said: "How does one recognize the dharma of non-duality?"
Mañjuśrī said: "If there were no duality to be cognized, then it would not be non-dual. Why is this so? Because..."
That which is without dual characteristics cannot be cognized. Brahmā!
Duality is the activity of cognition; that which is not a dharma of cognition is what the Buddha has taught.
This Dharma is not as it has been described. Why is this?
Because this Dharma is without words or letters.
“Mañjuśrī! To what ultimate destination does the Dharma taught by the Buddha lead? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha reaches that which has nowhere to reach. Brahmā said,
"Does the Dharma taught by the Buddha not reach nirvāṇa?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Can one reach it within nirvāṇa?
The Brahmā replied:
“Nirvāṇa has no place from which it comes and no place to which it goes. Mañjuśrī said, “So it is!”
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha reaches that which has nowhere to reach. Brahmā said:
"Who listens to this Dharma?"
He replied, "As you have said. Brahmā said:
"What does 'as it was spoken' mean? He replied,
"It means as if one neither recognizes nor hears."
Brahmā said: "Who is able to listen to such a Dharma as this from the Tathāgata? He replied:
"Regarding 'not leaking into the six sense objects,' the Brahmā said:
'Who is able to know this Dharma?'"
He replied, “It is one who is without consciousness, without discrimination,
and without contention. Brahmā said:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who is full of contention? He replied:
"'This is good,' 'this is evil'—this is called contention."
"This is principle" and "this is non-principle"—this is called contention;
"this is defilement" and "this is purity"—this is called contention;
"this is wholesome" and "this is unwholesome"—this is called contention.
"This is upholding the precepts; this is violating the precepts"—this is called contention.
"This should be done; this should not be done"—this is called contention.
"By means of this dharma one attains the Way; by means of this dharma one attains the fruit"—this is called contention.
"Brahmā! If within the Dharma there is a sense of high or low, or if one is greedily attached to grasping and receiving, all such things constitute contention;
that which the Buddha has taught is free from contention."
Brahmā! Those who delight in conceptual proliferation do not refrain from contention; those who delight in contention possess no qualities of a śramaṇa;
and those who delight in the qualities of a śramaṇa are free from deluded thoughts and greedy attachments.
Brahmā said: "In what way does a bhikṣu follow the Buddha’s words and follow the Buddha’s teachings? He replied:
"If a bhikṣu remains unmoved in mind whether praised or reviled, this is called following the Buddha's teaching;
if a bhikṣu does not follow literal words and phrases, this is called following the Buddha's word."
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu extinguishes all signs, this is called following the Buddha’s teaching;
when he does not contradict the meaning, this is called following the Buddha’s word.
If a bhikṣu guards the Dharma, this is called following the Buddha’s teaching.
"Not contradicting the Buddha’s words—this is called following the Buddha’s words. Brahmā said:
"How can a bhikṣu protect the Dharma?"
He replied, "If a bhikṣu does not oppose equality and does not destroy the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is called being able to protect the Dharma. Brahmā said:
“How does a bhikṣu draw near to the Buddha? He replied:
“If a bhikṣu, among all phenomena, does not perceive any phenomenon as being either near or far, this is called drawing near to the Buddha.”
The Brahmā said, "In what way does a bhikṣu serve the Buddha? He replied:
“If a bhikṣu performs no action of body, speech, or mind, this is called serving the Buddha.
Brahmā said: “Who is able to make offerings to the Buddha?”
He replied, "If one does not give rise to meritorious karma, nor give rise to immovable karma. Brahmā said:
"Who is able to see the Buddha?
He replied, "If one does not cling to the fleshly eye, does not cling to the divine eye, and does not cling to the wisdom eye, this is called being able to see the Buddha."
Brahmā said: "Who is able to see the Dharma? He replied:
"One who does not oppose the principle of all causes and conditions. Brahmā said:
"Who is able to see all causes and conditions in accordance with reality?"
He replied, "It is because one does not give rise to equanimity, nor perceive the characteristics produced by equanimity. Brahmā said:
"Who attains true wisdom?
He replied, "Those whose various outflows (āsrava) are neither produced nor extinguished."
Brahmā said: "Who is able to follow and learn from the Tathāgata? He replied:
"One who does not give rise to, does not receive, does not grasp, and does not abandon any phenomena.
Brahmā said: "Who is called one of right practice?"
He replied, "One who does not fall into the three realms. Brahmā said:
"Who is a virtuous person?
He replied, "One who does not undergo further rebirth."
Brahmā said, "Who is the person who finds joy? He replied:
"One who is without self and without what belongs to a self.
Brahmā said: "Who is it that attains liberation?"
He replied, "One who does not destroy the fetters. Brahmā said:
"Who is it that has attained deliverance? He replied,
"One who dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa."
The Brahmā said:
"What has the bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted exhausted? He replied:
"If there were something that could be exhausted, it would not be called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
To know that all outflows have the characteristic of emptiness, and to accord with such knowledge, is called the exhaustion of outflows. Brahmā said:
"Who speaks the truth?
He replied, "One who has departed from all paths of verbal discourse."
Brahmā said, "Who enters the Path? He replied:
"If an ordinary person practices the path of entering the noble way, knowing that all conditioned phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere, then they have entered the Way."
Brahmā said, "Who is able to see the noble truths? He replied:
"There is no one who sees the Noble Truths. Why is this?
For whatever views there may be, they are all false; it is only when there is nothing seen that one is said to see the Truth."
Brahmā said: "Not seeing what dharma is called 'seeing the truth'? He replied:
"Not seeing any views whatsoever is called 'seeing the truth.
The Brahmā said: "Where should this truth be sought?"
He replied: "One should seek it within the four inversions. Brahmā said:
"Why do you speak thus? He replied:
"Seeking the four perversions, one does not find purity, does not find permanence, does not find bliss, and does not find self."
If purity cannot be attained, that is itself impurity;
if permanence cannot be attained, that is itself impermanence;
if happiness cannot be attained, that is itself suffering.
If one does not apprehend a self, then there is no self. Brahmā!
That all dharmas are empty and without self is the Noble Truth.
"If one seeks the truths in such a manner, this person does not perceive suffering, does not abandon the origin, does not realize cessation, and does not cultivate the path.
Brahmā asked: "What is meant by 'cultivating the path'?"
He replied: "If one does not discriminate between what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and remains free from these two marks, this is called cultivating the path;
because one seeks all dharmas through this path and finds them not, this is called the path."
This Path does not cause one to leave birth-and-death to reach Nirvana.
Why is this? It is precisely because it does not involve leaving or reaching that it is called the Noble Path.
At that time, there was a Mahallaka Brahma-son named Samacārin who asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is meant by a lay follower (upāsaka) taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha?"

He replied: "An upāsaka does not give rise to two views—he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of another; he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Buddha; he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Dharma; he does not give rise to the view of self nor the view of the Saṅgha. This is called taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha."
Furthermore, an upāsaka does not see the Buddha through form, nor does he see the Buddha through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; this is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
An upāsaka makes no conceptual distinctions regarding phenomena (*dharma*), nor does he practice what is contrary to the Dharma; this is called taking refuge in the Dharma.

If an upāsaka does not perceive the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-dharma) apart from the conditioned (saṃskṛta-dharma), nor perceive the conditioned apart from the unconditioned, this is called taking refuge in the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, when a lay follower does not perceive a Buddha, does not perceive the Dharma, and does not perceive the Saṅgha, this is called taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin asked Mañjuśrī,
“Where do these bodhisattvas who have resolved upon awakening (bodhicitta) head toward?”
He replied: "It proceeds toward empty space. Why is this so? Because..."
"Because *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is identical to empty space. Samacārin asked:
"In what sense is a bodhisattva said to have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

He replied: "If a bodhisattva knows that all arousal [of the mind] is non-arousal, that all phenomena are non-phenomena, and that all sentient beings are non-sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called a ‘bodhisattva,’ what is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva’?”
The Buddha said,

“Good son! If a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings fixed in error, yet perceives no distinction between them and those fixed in correctness, he is therefore called a bodhisattva.”

Why is this? It is because a bodhisattva does not resolve their mind for the sake of those beings fixed in the right [path], nor for the sake of those of indeterminate nature; rather, it is solely for the sake of delivering those beings fixed in the wrong [path] that they give rise to great compassion and resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, they are called "bodhisattvas."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin addressed the Buddha, saying: [From here below, according to the Dan edition, this is the thirteenth chapter, "The Meaning of Names. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bodhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We also wish to explain why one is called a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said, "Speak then!"
The Bodhisattva Bodhi said:
"For example, if a man or a woman receives the one-day precepts (upavāsa) and maintains them without violation or deficiency;

if a bodhisattva likewise, from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, constantly cultivates pure conduct throughout that interval, he is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati said:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes a profound and firm mind of loving-kindness, he is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sattvatāraṇa said:
"It is like a bridge or a boat that ferries people across without weariness and without discrimination; if the mind is thus, one is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Severing Evil Paths said:
"If, wherever a bodhisattva places his foot in any buddha-field, all evil paths are immediately extinguished, he is called a bodhisattva."
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said:
"If sentient beings see this Bodhisattva, they shall immediately become fixed in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
furthermore, those who invoke his name shall be freed from all sufferings—this is what is called a 'Bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said:
"If wherever a bodhisattva sets foot causes the three-thousandfold world system and the palaces of Māra to tremble, he is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Aśrānta said:
"If a period of Ganges-sand-like eons were made into one day and night, and thirty such days were made into a month, and twelve such months into a year;
and if, by this reckoning of years, one were to encounter a single Buddha only after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons;"

Thus, having practiced the various holy lives and accumulated merit under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one subsequently receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; with a mind that never ceases and remains free from weariness, such a person is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Guide said:
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings who have fallen onto wrong paths, leading them to enter the right path without seeking any reward, this is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Sumeru said:
"If a bodhisattva makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena, being as singular among all forms as Mount Sumeru, he is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"If a bodhisattva is not destroyed by any afflictions, he is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Cittabala said:
"If a bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas with the mind without error, this is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Lion’s Gait Sovereign said:

"If a bodhisattva, amidst various treatises, is neither terrified nor afraid and attains profound dharma-patience, such that he can cause all non-Buddhists to be terrified, this is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Acintya said: “If a bodhisattva knows that the characteristics of the mind are inconceivable and is free from all thought and discrimination, he is called a bodhisattva.”
The Devaputra Śāntipraśānta said:
"If a bodhisattva is able to be born within all celestial palaces without being stained, and yet does not even apprehend this state of being unstained, they are called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Satyavādin said:
"If a bodhisattva always speaks with truth whenever he utters words, and even in his dreams does not speak falsely, he is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said,
“If a bodhisattva can see that all forms are the form of the Buddha, this is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sadāparitrāṇa said:

"If a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings fallen into birth and death, finds no delight in the various pleasures of the world, and desires to deliver both himself and other sentient beings, this is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind said:
"If a bodhisattva does not feel anger or obstruction toward any afflictions or māras, this is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Joyful Faculty said:
"If a bodhisattva always fulfills their own vows with roots of goodness and also fulfills the vows of others, accomplishing all that is to be done, they are called a 'bodhisattva'.
The Bodhisattva Dispelling Doubt said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to doubt or regret regarding any phenomena, they are called a 'bodhisattva'."
The Bodhisattva Lion Maiden said:

"If a bodhisattva is without male characteristics and without female characteristics, yet manifests various physical forms for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, this is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāvatī said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to attachment or delight toward worldly treasures, but delights only in the Three Jewels, they are called a bodhisattva."
The upāsikā Viśākhā Dattā said: “If a bodhisattva has anything to attain, there is no bodhi.
One who does not attain any dharma, does not give rise to any dharma, and does not extinguish any dharma is called a bodhisattva.”
The lay follower Bhadrapāla said:
"If sentient beings hear the name of a bodhisattva, they will certainly attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment; such a person is called a bodhisattva."
The youth Ratnacandra said:
"If a bodhisattva constantly cultivates the celibate conduct of a youth, such that he does not even mentally conceive of the five desires, how much less would he experience them with his body!"
"This is called a Bodhisattva.
The Devaputra Māndāravapuṣpa-gandha-bodhisattva said:
"If a Bodhisattva perfumes the mind with the observance of precepts, constantly emitting the fragrance of all wholesome dharmas and not emitting any other fragrance, this is called a Bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Joy-Maker said:
"If a bodhisattva delights in three dharmas—namely, making offerings to the Buddha, expounding the Dharma, and transforming sentient beings—he is called a bodhisattva."
The Brahma Heaven King Viśeṣacintin said:
"If whatever dharmas a bodhisattva perceives are all the Buddha-dharma, this is called a bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
"If a bodhisattva is one whom sentient beings see and immediately attain the samādhi of loving-kindness, this is called a bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, said:
"If a bodhisattva, though preaching all dharmas, does not give rise to the mark of dharmas nor give rise to the mark of non-dharmas, this is called a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha said:
"If a bodhisattva’s radiance can extinguish the afflictions of all sentient beings, he is called a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Samantakusuma said:
"If a bodhisattva sees all Tathāgatas filling the worlds of the ten directions like flowers blooming in a forest, this is called a bodhisattva.
Thus, each of these bodhisattvas spoke according to their own inclination.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:

"If a bodhisattva can undergo all manner of suffering and affliction on behalf of all sentient beings, and can likewise relinquish all meritorious deeds to give them to all sentient beings, this one is called a bodhisattva."
Chapter 8: On Tranquility (3). Chapter Eight: On Tranquility. At that time, Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Bodhisattva Samacaryā, saying: "Good son!
"With what kind of conduct do you now practice? He replied,
"I practice with the conduct of all sentient beings who follow conditioned phenomena."
He asked again:
"In accordance with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), by what do sentient beings act? He replied:
“The conduct of all Buddhas is the conduct of all sentient beings who follow conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
He asked again:
“By what do all Buddhas conduct themselves?”
He replied, “The Buddhas take the emptiness of the ultimate truth as their practice.
He asked again:
"If the practices of ordinary beings are the same as those of the Buddhas, what difference is there between them? Samatācaryā replied,
"Do you wish to find a difference within emptiness?"
He replied, "No. Samacārin said:
“Does the Tathāgata not teach that all phenomena are empty?
He replied, “Indeed he does.”
"Therefore, Brahmā! All dharmas are without distinction;
these characteristics of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are likewise so. Why is this?
“The Tathāgata does not say that there are distinctions among all dharmas.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is meant by the so-called ‘practice of practice’?”
He replied: "Within all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), there are four sublime abodes (brahmavihāra); these are called 'practicing the sphere of practice.
If a person is devoid of the four sublime abodes, they are not said to be practicing the sphere of practice."
To be able to practice the four brahma-vihāras is called "practicing the sphere of conduct. O Brahmā!
If a person accomplishes the four brahma-vihāras, even if they travel through empty and desolate wildernesses, this is called "practicing the sphere of conduct."

If one does not accomplish the four brahma-vihāras, then even if one walks among multi-storied pavilions, halls, towers, and galleries, or upon couches and beds of gold and silver with exquisite coverlets and bedding, this is not called "walking in the proper place," nor can one rightly know the characteristics of the proper place.
He asked again:
"By what conduct does a bodhisattva bring about the purification of their knowledge and vision? He replied:
"One can purify the view of self within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
He asked again:
"If one attains the true nature of the self, does one thereby attain true knowledge and vision?"
He replied: "Indeed!
If one perceives my true nature, that is precisely what constitutes true knowledge and vision."
For example, just as a king’s treasurer, by means of what has already been disbursed and used, knows what remains;
so too, by means of knowing my true nature, one attains true knowledge and vision.
He asked again:
"How does one realize the true nature of the self? He replied:
“If one attains the dharma of non-self. Why is this?
Because the self ultimately has no root and no fixed existence.”
"If one can know in this way, this is called attaining the true nature of the self.
He asked again:
"As I understand the meaning of what Mañjuśrī has said, by seeing the self, one sees the Buddha."
Why is this? Because my own nature is itself the Buddha-nature, Mañjuśrī!
"Who is able to see the Buddha?
He replied, "One who does not destroy the view of a self."
"Why is this? The view of self is itself the view of dharmas; it is by means of the view of dharmas that one can see the Buddha.
He asked again:
“Is there such a thing as ‘non-practice’ that is called ‘right practice’? He replied, “There is.”
"If one does not engage in any conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), this is called right practice.
He asked again:
"What kind of practice is called right practice?"
He replied: "If one practices not for the sake of seeing, not for the sake of abandoning, not for the sake of realizing, and not for the sake of cultivating, this is called right practice."
He asked again:
"What dharmas does the wisdom-eye perceive? He replied:
"If there is anything seen, it is not called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
The wisdom-eye sees neither conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) nor unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Why is this so? "
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are false conceptualizations; the absence of false conceptualization is called the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are empty and non-existent, transcending the paths of all eyes; therefore, the eye of wisdom likewise does not see unconditioned phenomena.
He asked again:
"Is there any cause or condition by which a bhikṣu who practices correctly might not attain the fruits of the path? He replied:
“There is! Within right practice, there is no path, no fruit, no practice, no attainment, and no distinction of attaining a fruit. Brahmā!”
Because there is nothing to be attained, it is called "attainment.
If there were anything to be attained, one should know that such a person is one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
One who practices correctly has no overweening pride; having no overweening pride, there is neither practice nor attainment.
He asked again:
"By attaining what dharma is one said to have attained the Way? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If a dharma is not self-arisen, not other-arisen, nor arisen from a multitude of conditions, and has been eternally without arising from the very beginning—because one attains such a dharma, it is called 'attaining the Way.'"
He asked again:
"If a dharma is unarisen, what can be attained? He replied:
"If one knows that dharmas are unarisen, this is precisely what is called 'attainment. Therefore, the Buddha said:
'If one sees that all conditioned dharmas have the characteristic of non-arising, one immediately enters the stage of certainty.'"
He asked again: "What is called the 'right position'? He replied:
"To not differentiate between 'self' and 'nirvāṇa' as two is called the state of rightness (*samyaktva*).
Furthermore, because one practices equality, it is called the state of rightness.
Because one emerges from all suffering and affliction through equality, it is called the state of rightness."
"Because one has entered into the definitive meaning, it is called the 'right position.
Because all recollections have been eliminated, it is called the 'right position.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! You have spoken these words most skillfully; it is truly as you have said.
When this Dharma was being taught, seven thousand bhikṣus were no longer grasping at any phenomena; their outflows were exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
Thirty-two thousand devas were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;

ten thousand people became free from desire and attained meditative concentration; two hundred people resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; and five hundred bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Brahma-king Cintavistara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī is able to perform the work of a Buddha, greatly benefiting sentient beings.”
Mañjuśrī said: "The Buddha appears in the world not for the sake of increasing dharmas, nor does he appear for the sake of diminishing dharmas. Brahmā said:
“Does not the Buddha bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa?
Does the Venerable One also not benefit immeasurable sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Do you wish to obtain a sentient being within that which is devoid of sentient beings? He replied, "No!"
“Brahmā! Do you wish to obtain a definitive characteristic of sentient beings? He replied:
"No, Brahmā! Do you wish for the Buddhas to have the characteristic of birth in the world?"
He replied, “No, Brahmā! “Brahmā! [he continued].
"Who are those sentient beings who are liberated by the Buddha?
Brahmā replied, "According to the meaning of what you have said, there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa."
Mañjuśrī said: “It is so! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not attain birth-and-death, nor do they attain nirvāṇa.”
The disciples of the Buddha who have attained liberation likewise neither attain birth-and-death nor attain nirvāṇa.
Why is this? This nirvāṇa and this birth-and-death exist merely as provisional names and verbal designations!
"In reality, there is no coming and going in birth and death, nor is there the attainment of nirvana through extinction.
He asked again:
"Who is able to believe in this Dharma?"
He replied, "One who has no attachment among all phenomena.
He asked again:
"If one is greedily attached, to what is one greedily attached?
He replied, "One is greedily attached to the false."
"Brahmā! If one were attached to this as being real, there would ultimately be no person of overweening pride;
because one is attached to what is false, the practitioner knows it for what it is and does not become attached."
If there is no greedy attachment, then there are no outflows;
if there are no outflows, then there is no coming and going in birth and death;
if there is no coming and going in birth and death, this is nirvāṇa.
He asked again:
"For what reason do you speak of 'extinction' (nirvāṇa)? He replied:
"Nirvāṇa is defined as the non-conjunction of various conditions.
If ignorance does not conjoin with the causal conditions for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), then volitional formations do not arise;
if volitional formations do not arise, this is called cessation. This characteristic of non-arising is ultimate cessation."
"Because one attains this Way, there is no place of birth; this is what is called the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Is all that you have spoken truly real?"
He replied, "All speech is entirely true.
He asked again:
"Is false speech also true? He replied, "It is so!"
Why is this so? Because all these verbal expressions are false and illusory, having no location and no direction.
If all phenomena are false and illusory, having neither location nor direction, then for this reason, all verbal expressions are themselves true.
"Good son! The speech of Devadatta and the speech of the Tathāgata are neither different nor distinct. Why is this so?
All verbal expressions are the verbal expressions of the Tathāgata, for they do not depart from suchness.

All verbal expressions have objects that are spoken of; yet it is precisely because there is nothing to be spoken of that there can be anything spoken of. Therefore, all verbal expressions are equal, because their characters are identical, because characters are without conceptualization, and because characters are empty.
Samacārin asked, “Does the Tathāgata not speak of both the speech of ordinary persons and the speech of noble ones? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Indeed! One uses written characters to express the speech of ordinary worldlings, and one also uses written characters to express the speech of noble sages.
Thus it is, good son!"
"Are these various syllables and letters subject to discrimination? Are they the speech of ordinary worldlings, or the speech of the noble ones?
Samacārin replied, "No!"
Mañjuśrī said: "Just as all letters are without discrimination, so too are all noble ones (ārya) without discrimination; therefore, the noble ones have no speech."
Why is this? Because the noble ones do not speak by means of the mark of letters, nor by the mark of sentient beings, nor by the mark of dharmas.
It is like a bell or a drum, which produces sound through the conjunction of various conditions; yet these bells and drums themselves possess no discrimination.
"Thus, because these worthy noble ones thoroughly understand the various causes and conditions, they are without attachment and without obstruction regarding all verbal expressions.
Equal Practice said:
"As the Buddha has taught:"
"You, having gathered in assembly, should practice two things: either preaching the Dharma or noble silence.
What is meant by preaching the Dharma?
What is meant by noble silence?
He replied: "If one preaches the Dharma without contradicting the Buddha, without contradicting the Dharma, and without contradicting the Sangha, this is called preaching the Dharma.
If one knows that the Dharma is itself the Buddha, that detachment from marks is itself the Dharma, and that the unconditioned is itself the Sangha, this is called noble silence."
Furthermore, son of good family!
To speak on account of the four foundations of mindfulness is called "teaching the Dharma";
to have no recollection or thought regarding any phenomena is called "noble silence."
To speak on account of the four right efforts is called "teaching the Dharma";
because all dharmas are equal, neither creating equality nor creating inequality, it is called "noble silence."
To speak based on the four bases of psychic power is called "teaching the Dharma";
if one does not give rise to body or mind, it is called "noble silence.
To speak based on the five faculties and the five powers is called "teaching the Dharma."

If one has faith that does not follow the words of others, and for the sake of neither grasping nor rejecting, discriminates among all phenomena while dwelling single-mindedly in tranquility; if within every moment of thought one understands all phenomena, possessing the wisdom of constant determination that cuts off all conceptual proliferation—this is called "noble silence."
To have something spoken based on the seven factors of enlightenment is called "teaching the Dharma";
if one constantly practices equanimity, without discrimination, and without increase or decrease, it is called "noble silence."
To speak on account of the eight factors of the noble path is called "teaching the Dharma";
if one knows that the characteristics of teaching the Dharma are like the parable of the raft—neither relying on the Dharma nor relying on what is not the Dharma—it is called "noble silence."
"Good son! If one can explain and expound these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), it is called 'preaching the Dharma.

If one personally realizes these dharmas, yet does not see the dharma apart from the body, nor sees the body apart from the dharma—within this contemplation seeing neither the mark of duality nor the mark of non-duality—and thus knows and sees them as they manifest before one, yet even this knowing and seeing is not seen, it is called 'noble silence' (*ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva*)."
Furthermore, son of good family!

If one does not falsely conceptualize and cling to a self, does not falsely conceptualize and cling to others, and does not falsely conceptualize and cling to dharmas as having something to be spoken, this is called "preaching the Dharma.
If one reaches the state of the ineffable, is able to transcend all speech and sound, attains the unmoving ground, and enters the mind free from signs, this is called "noble silence."
Furthermore, noble son!
To know the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings and to instruct them accordingly is called "preaching the Dharma";
to constantly enter meditative concentration with an undistracted mind is called "noble silence."
Samacārin said: "As I understand the meaning of what Mañjuśrī has spoken, among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, there is neither the preaching of the Dharma nor noble silence."
Why is this? Because they are unable to discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, nor are they able to remain constantly in meditative concentration. Mañjuśrī!
If there should be one who asks in truth:
"Who is the one in the world who speaks the Dharma?
Who is the one in the world who maintains noble silence?"
"In that case, one should explain that it is the Buddhas who are so. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas are well able to discern the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings, and they are also constantly in meditative concentration."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is, so it is!
Just as Saṃcārin has said, only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess these two dharmas.”
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have personally heard from the Buddha:"
"You all, having assembled, should practice two things: either preaching the Dharma or noble silence.
World-Honored One!
If the śrāvakas are unable to practice these, why does the Tathāgata command the bhikṣus to practice these two things?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
If a śrāvaka were not to hear it from another, would he be able to preach the Dharma or to maintain noble silence?"
Subhūti replied, “No, [World-Honored One]. “Subhūti! [the Buddha said.]
"Therefore, you should know that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have neither the preaching of Dharma nor noble silence.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Subhūti, saying: "Elder Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of sentient beings.
Do you possess the wisdom within this regard to be able to preach the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each?
He replied, “No! [The Buddha asked:

“Now, Subhūti, can you enter the samādhi that contemplates the minds of all sentient beings? Abiding in this samādhi, do you penetrate the minds and mental activities of all sentient beings, such that there is no obstruction between your own mind and the minds of others?”
He replied, “No, Subhūti! “Subhūti! [the Buddha continued.]
The Tathāgata, regarding the eighty-four thousand modes of conduct among sentient beings, preaches the medicine of the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each.

Furthermore, while abiding eternally in a state of meditative concentration characterized by equanimity, his mind remains unshaken as he penetrates the mental activities and mental factors of all sentient beings.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not equal this matter. Subhūti!
There may be sentient beings who have much lust and attain liberation through the contemplation of the pure rather than the impure—only a Buddha can know this.
There may be sentient beings who have much anger and attain liberation through the contemplation of faults rather than through a mind of loving-kindness—only a Buddha can know this.
There may be sentient beings who possess much ignorance and attain liberation through not being addressed, rather than through the preaching of the Dharma—only a Buddha can know this.

There may be sentient beings with balanced faculties (samabhāga) who do not attain liberation through contemplating the pure, nor through contemplating the impure, nor through contemplating faults, nor through a mind of loving-kindness, nor through not being addressed, nor through the preaching of the Dharma; for them, the Buddha preaches the Dharma according to their specific faculties by means of the equality of all phenomena so that they may attain liberation—only a Buddha can know this.
"Therefore, among all those who preach the Dharma, the Tathāgata is the foremost; and among those who dwell in meditative concentration, he is also the foremost.

At that time, Subhūti asked Mañjuśrī, "If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to preach the Dharma in this way and unable to maintain such noble silence, do bodhisattvas possess such meritorious qualities as to be able to preach the Dharma and to maintain noble silence?"
He replied, "Only the Buddha should know this!
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“There is a samādhi named ‘Entering All Languages with an Undistracted Mind’; if a bodhisattva accomplishes this samādhi, they shall all obtain these merits.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin: “Good son!
To address the eighty-four thousand types of conduct among sentient beings, one expounds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma; this is called "preaching the Dharma.
To constantly abide in all meditative concentrations that extinguish sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is called "noble silence."

"Good son! Even if I were to spend an eon, or slightly less than an eon, to explain this meaning—namely, the characteristics of preaching the Dharma and the characteristics of noble silence—I would still not be able to exhaust it."
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin: "Good son!

In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Samantaprabha; the kalpa was called Yaśasvin, and the land was named Priyadarśana."

That land is majestic, pure, abundant, prosperous, peaceful, and secure; devas and humans flourish there. Its ground is adorned with various jewels, soft and smooth, where precious lotus flowers grow. It is filled with all kinds of fragrant trees that constantly emit exquisite scents.
"Good son! In the land of Priyadarśana, there are forty billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*), and each four-continent world is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Within them, the various cities are one yojana in length and breadth, all adorned with various jewels."
Each city was surrounded by fifteen thousand villages and towns.
Within each village and town, there were hundreds of thousands of people filling them to capacity.

At that time, the forms and appearances perceived by the people all brought joy to their hearts; there was nothing loathsome, and they all attained the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). For this reason, the land was named "Joyful Vision" (Kṣema-darśana).
If the bodhisattvas who have come from other worlds all obtain happiness, it is not so in other lands.
Good son! That Buddha Samantaraśmi teaches the Dharma of the three vehicles to his disciples, and he also frequently delights in proclaiming such sounds of the Dharma:
"O bhikṣus, you should practice two things:
either preaching the Dharma or noble silence. "Good son!"
At that time, there were two bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of the Medicine King Buddha in the zenith:
one named Akṣayamati and the other named Upakāramati; they came to the presence of the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa.
They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, joining their palms in reverence, withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhāsa) extensively expounded the Samādhi of Pure Radiance for the two bodhisattvas:

"The reason it is called the Samādhi of Pure Radiance is that if a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they immediately attain liberation from all signs and attachments to afflictions, and also obtain pure radiance regarding all Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is named the Samādhi of Pure Radiance."

Furthermore, all phenomena are pure in the past limit, pure in the future limit, and pure in the present; these three times are ultimately pure, for nothing can render them impure, as their nature is eternally pure. Therefore, it is said that the nature of all phenomena is eternally clear and pure.
What is meant by the intrinsic purity of all phenomena?
It means that all phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness, because they are free from anything to be apprehended;
all phenomena have the characteristic of signlessness, because they are free from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination.

All dharmas have the characteristic of non-action; they are neither grasped nor abandoned, and are without seeking or aspiration, because they are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature. This is called the eternal purity of nature.

By means of this mark of constant purity, one knows that the nature of birth and death is itself nirvāṇa, and that the nature of nirvāṇa is itself the nature of all phenomena; therefore, it is said that the nature of the mind is eternally pure.
"Good son! For example, it is impossible for space to become defiled;
likewise, it is impossible for the nature of the mind to be defiled."
Furthermore, it is like space: although it may be obscured by smoke, dust, clouds, and mist, becoming dim and impure, it cannot defile the nature of space.
Even if it were defiled, it could never be made impure forever, because space is in reality undefiled; thus, it is seen as pure once again.
The mind of an ordinary person is also like this: although various afflictions arise through false recollection, the characteristic of that mind cannot be defiled;
even if it were defiled, it could not be purified again, because the characteristic of the mind is in reality undefiled, its nature being eternally luminous and pure.
Therefore, the mind attains liberation.
Good son! This is called entering the gate of the Samādhi of Pure Radiance.
When those two bodhisattvas heard this samādhi, they attained the inconceivable light of the Dharma regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha Samantaprabhā, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“We have already heard about entering the gate of the Samādhi of Pure Radiance.
By what practice should we practice this Dharma-gate?
The Buddha told Akṣayamati:
“Sons of good family!
You should practice two modes of conduct:
either preaching the Dharma or noble silence.”

Then the two bodhisattvas, having received the instruction from the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. They proceeded to a grove where, by their own supernatural power, they manifested jeweled towers within which they practiced cultivation.

At that time, there was a Brahmā named Subhāṣitaghoṣa, who, together with seventy-two thousand Brahmās, came to where [the two bodhisattvas] were, prostrated at their feet with his head, and asked the two bodhisattvas:
"O sons of good family!..."
The Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa said:
"You bhikṣus, when assembled, should practice two things:
either preaching the Dharma or noble silence."
"Good son! What is called 'preaching the Dharma,' and what is called 'noble silence'?"
The two bodhisattvas said:
"Listen well now; we shall speak briefly, for only the Tathāgata fully comprehends this!
Thereupon, the two bodhisattvas extensively analyzed and explained the meaning of these two phrases for the assembly of Brahmās."

At that time, seventy-two thousand Brahmās all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Brahmā Sublime Light attained the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.

These two bodhisattvas, for seventy-six thousand years, answered his questions with the power of unimpeded eloquence; they tirelessly and without ceasing analyzed the two phrases, engaging in mutual dialogue that was inexhaustible.
Thereupon, the Buddha Samantaprabha, situated in the midst of space, spoke these words:
"Good son! Do not give rise to contention over written words or verbal expressions!"
All verbal expressions are empty and like echoes; as the question was, so too is the answer.
You two have both attained unimpeded eloquence and the inexhaustible dhāraṇī; whether for one kalpa or a hundred kalpas, you could not exhaust the eloquence required to explain these two phrases.
"Good son! The Buddha-dharma is the foremost meaning of the characteristic of quiescence; herein there are no words, and it cannot be expressed in speech.
All that is spoken possesses no ultimate benefit."
"Therefore, you all should follow this meaning and not follow the literal words.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the two bodhisattvas fell silent.
The Buddha then addressed Samantagāmin:

"By this you should know that if a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma with eloquence, it could not be exhausted even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, or even beyond hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas."
He further addressed Samantagamin:
"What do you think? Are those two bodhisattvas anyone other than these very persons?
Do not conceive such a view!"
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati is now Mañjuśrī; the Bodhisattva Upakāśa is now your own self; and the Brahmā Prabhāsa is now the Brahmā Śikṣānanda.

Chapter 9: On Diligent Practice (3). [Note: This chapter is absent from the Danzang edition; at the end of the scroll, following the passage "At that time Mañjuśrī... down to the sixteenth chapter, "On Attaining the Holy Path," there is a marginal note stating: "At the end of the scroll, this corresponds to the nineteenth line on the left side of the page in the current edition. At that time, the Bodhisattva Samacārin addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is unprecedented!
"Bhagavān! The bodhi of all Buddhas brings great benefit to those sentient beings who practice with diligence as it has been taught."
World-Honored One!

Those who are indolent and unable to practice according to the teaching can achieve nothing, even if they encounter hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas. You should know that bodhi is attained through diligent and energetic effort.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Samacārin:
"Good son, do you know how a bodhisattva practices so as to be called 'diligently energetic'?"
He replied: "If a bodhisattva is able to attain the noble path, this is called diligent vigor.
He asked again:
“How can one practice so as to attain the Noble Path? He replied,
“If one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, such a practitioner can attain the Noble Path.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'having attained the noble path'? He replied:
"If a practitioner perceives the equality of all phenomena within equality, this is called having attained the Noble Path.
He asked again:
"Can equality be perceived?"
He replied, “No. Why is that? Because...”
"If that which is visible as equal were truly equal,
it would not be equal. The Brahmā Viśeṣacintin said to Mañjuśrī,
"If a practitioner does not perceive any phenomena within equality, this is called having attained the Noble Path."
Mañjuśrī said: "For what reason do you not see it? Siyi replied:
"Because one is detached from the two marks, there is no seeing; this very non-seeing is right seeing.
He asked again:
"Who is able to see the world correctly?"
He replied, "One who does not destroy the characteristics of the world.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not destroying the characteristics of the world'? He replied:
"Form and suchness are without distinction or difference; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and suchness are without distinction or difference."
"If a practitioner perceives the five aggregates as equal and according to their true nature, this is called 'rightly seeing the world.
He asked again:
"What is the characteristic of the world?"
He replied, “Cessation is the characteristic of the world.
He asked again:
"Can the characteristic of cessation itself be exhausted? He replied,
"The characteristic of cessation cannot be exhausted."
He asked again:
"For what reason do you say:
'The world has the characteristic of cessation'?"
He replied: "The world has the characteristic of ultimate exhaustion, yet this characteristic cannot be exhausted. Why is that?
"That which has already been exhausted is not to be exhausted again.
He asked again:
"Does the Buddha not say that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) have the characteristic of exhaustion?"
He replied: "The world has the characteristic of exhaustion, yet it can never be exhausted.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all conditioned phenomena have the characteristic of exhaustion."
He asked again:
"For what reason are they frequently called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)? He replied:
"Because they possess the characteristic of exhaustion, they are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
He asked again:
"In what do conditioned phenomena abide?"
He replied, "I abide within the nature of the unconditioned.
He asked again:
"What is the distinction between conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)? He replied:
"Between conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena, there is only a distinction in terms of letters and verbal expression!"
Why is this so? Because through words and speech, one speaks of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Yet, if one seeks the true mark (*dharmatā*) of both the conditioned and the unconditioned, there is no distinction between them, for the true mark is itself without distinction.
He asked again:
"What is the meaning of the true mark of all dharmas? He replied:
"All phenomena are equal and without distinction; this is the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'meaning'?"
He replied: "It is called 'meaning' because it is explained through words and letters so that people may attain understanding. Why is this so?
The meaning of the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is not as it is expressed by words.
Although the Buddhas employ words to speak, there is no increase or decrease in the true reality.

Mañjuśrī! All verbal expressions are, in truth, not verbal expressions; therefore, the Buddha’s speech is called "inexpressible," for the Buddhas cannot be described by means of the characteristics of words.
He asked again:
"How can one speak of the marks of a Buddha? He replied:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot be described by means of their physical bodies; they cannot be described by means of the thirty-two marks; nor can they be described by means of their various meritorious qualities."
He asked again:
"Can the Buddhas describe their marks apart from the form-body (rūpakāya), the thirty-two marks, and all the qualities of merit? He replied:
"No, it is not so! Why is this? Because the suchness of the form-body, the suchness of the thirty-two marks, and the suchness of all meritorious dharmas are [identical]."

"The Buddhas are not identical to suchness (*tathatā*), nor are they separate from suchness; it is in this way that the characteristics of a Buddha can be described, for they do not lose their suchness.
He asked again:
"For what reason are the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, called 'Buddhas'?"

He replied: "Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have thoroughly realized that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*), they are called Tathāgatas and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Chapter Ten: Aspiration for the Mahāyāna (3). Chapter Ten: Aspiration for the Mahāyāna (in the *Dān* [Tang] edition, Chapter Seventeen: Practice of the Mahāyāna). Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samacaryā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by a bodhisattva setting forth on the Great Vehicle?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The Bodhisattva does not destroy form, yet sets forth the resolve for bodhicitta;
knowing that form is itself bodhi, this is called practicing bodhi.
As it is with form, so it is with bodhi; they enter equally into the nature of suchness.”
Not destroying the nature of all phenomena—this is called practicing bodhi.
Not destroying the nature of all phenomena is the meaning of bodhi;
within this meaning of bodhi, there is also no bodhi.
To practice correctly according to the ultimate truth is what is called practicing for bodhi.
To seek bodhi while being deluded regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—those very aggregates, elements, and sense bases are it; apart from these, there is no bodhi.
If there are bodhisattvas who, regarding the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas,
neither grasp nor reject them, they are said to be practicing bodhi.
If they do not differentiate between what is dharma and what is non-dharma as being two, [they are practicing bodhi].
Nor can it be non-dual; this is called practicing bodhi.
If there is duality, it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); if there is no duality, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One who is free from these two extremes is called one who practices bodhi.
This person has transcended the stage of ordinary beings, yet does not enter the fixed position of the Dharma;
though not yet having attained the fruit, they are a sage.
They are a field of merit for the world, practicing worldly dharmas while remaining in the midst like a lotus flower.
Practicing the supreme path is what is called "walking the bodhi-way.
One traverses all that is traversed in the world,
yet attains liberation from all that the world clings to.
The Bodhisattva is fearless; he does not sink into the abyss of birth and death.
Without sorrow or weariness, he traverses the path to enlightenment.
Such a person is able to skillfully know the true nature of the reality of dharmas.
Therefore, one does not discriminate between what is dharma and what is non-dharma.
When practicing the Buddha-way, there is no dharma to be abandoned, nor is there any dharma to be accepted; this is called the characteristic of bodhi.
All phenomena are signless, just like space;
they never give rise to the thought: "This is the sign" or "this is that which possesses the sign.
Well-knowing the conduct of the world, they fully understand the power of skillful means.
Able to fulfill all the aspirations of sentient beings,
Ever abiding in equanimity and upholding the Buddha’s true Dharma,
Without any conceptualization whatsoever— this is the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Whether there be Buddhas or no Buddhas, this Dharma abides eternally in the world;
one who can thoroughly penetrate this characteristic is said to be a protector and upholder of the Dharma.
Having realized and understood the true nature of all phenomena and their meaning, [one attains liberation].
Abiding therein, they expound it for others.
Practicing the profound Dharma, they cannot be fathomed by Māra,
because such persons have no attachment to any phenomena.
One aspires for the wisdom of all Buddhas, yet does not cling even to that aspiration;
this wisdom, throughout the ten directions, cannot be found by seeking it.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is unimpeded, for it clings neither to phenomena nor to non-phenomena.
If one can remain unattached to this, one will ultimately attain the Buddha-way.
Those people who delight in goodness, through their giving, become increasingly exalted;
they relinquish all that they possess, yet their minds remain unshaken.
All phenomena cannot be abandoned, nor can they be grasped;
all worldly dharmas are fundamentally unattainable. One who knows that all phenomena possess neither the characteristic of giving nor the characteristic of abandoning—
These are called great donors, who perceive nothing within the Dharma.
Such Bodhisattvas do not conceive of "self" or "what belongs to self";
therefore, when practicing giving, they give rise to no thoughts of greed or attachment.
Whatever acts of giving there may be, all are dedicated to the Buddha-way;
yet in both giving and bodhi, one does not dwell in these two characteristics.
With a precept that is unconditioned and unarisen, one constantly abides within this.
Nor does one form this thought: "I abide in this observance of precepts.
The wise understand the characteristics of precepts as neither arising nor being produced;
therefore, their precepts are pure, just like space.
Contemplate the body as like a reflection in a mirror, and speech as like an echo;
the mind is like a magical illusion, and do not exalt yourself on account of the precepts.
With a mind that is always supple, abide peacefully in the nature of cessation.
Completely eliminating all evils, one attains mastery over wholesome dharmas.
Regarding both the observance and the violation of precepts, one perceives neither of these two characteristics;
seeing the nature of phenomena in this way, one maintains the untainted precepts.
Having already crossed to the shore of forbearance, they are able to endure all evils;
toward all classes of sentient beings, their minds are always equanimous.
All phenomena perish moment by moment; their nature never abides.
Within this, there is neither abuse nor honor;
even if his body were dismembered limb by limb, his mind would never waver.
Knowing that the mind is not within, it is likewise not without.
The body, enemies, and weapons—all arise from the four great elements;
yet within earth, water, fire, and wind, there has never been any injury or harm.
Having thoroughly understood this matter, one should always practice the dharma of patience.
The Bodhisattva practices in this way, such that sentient beings cannot move him.
With courageous and diligent vigor, he firmly abides in the Mahāyāna;
this person has no dependence whatsoever upon body or mind.
Although one knows the root of birth and death, its limit cannot be found;
yet for the sake of all sentient beings, one adorns great vows.
Since dharmas have no fixed arising, how could there be any characteristic of cessation?
The ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi) cannot be apprehended; it is taught for the sake of those who are inverted.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inconceivable, eternally abiding within the world.
If one can know it thus, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings who do not understand these characteristics of phenomena;
for their sake, he exerts diligent effort so that they may be freed from perversion.
The Buddhas never perceive a determinate characteristic in sentient beings.
Yet he propagates the fundamental vow; one should observe his power of diligence.
Contemplating all phenomena, he knows them all to be like illusions and transformations;
finding no mark of solidity, he views them as empty space.
From false conceptualization, attachment gives rise to suffering and affliction;
for this reason, I open the gates of the Dharma to enable entry into nirvana.
For their sake, I practice diligence, yet without violating the Dharma.
Because they have departed from both dharma and non-dharma, they constantly practice true diligence.
Having distanced themselves from such [worldly] conduct, they thoroughly realize the samādhi of non-contention;
dwelling alone without clamor, they are ever fearful of birth and death.
Delighting in dwelling in seclusion, like a rhinoceros with its single horn,
they sport in the various meditative concentrations and clearly master all supernormal powers.
Their minds always abide in equanimity, whether dwelling in empty hermitages or amidst villages.
With dignified conduct free from change, always delighting in meditative concentration;
possessing faith and understanding of the eternally settled Dharma, as well as tranquility and the outflow-free state,
their minds have attained liberation— therefore, they are called those who are eternally settled.
Abiding personally in the dharma of equality, they lead sentient beings by means of this;
because they do not deviate from the practice of equality, they are called those who are always in meditative concentration.
Their resolve and mindfulness are ever firm, never forgetting the bodhicitta.
They are also able to transform sentient beings; therefore, they are said to be always in meditative concentration.
Constantly mindful of all Buddhas, the true Dharma-nature body, and remaining far removed from the marks of the form body;
therefore, they are said to be always in meditative concentration.
Constantly practicing mindfulness of the Dharma, Just as the true nature of all phenomena is such that there is no recollection—
Therefore, one is said to be "always in meditative concentration.
Constantly practicing mindfulness of the Sangha, The Sangha is itself the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Transcending both the calculable and the incalculable, those who constantly enter into suchness see all the Buddhas of the ten directions and all classes of sentient beings;
yet within the realm of the eye and its objects, they never give rise to dualistic marks.
They are able to hear and receive all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas,
yet within the sounds heard by their ears, they do not give rise to dualistic perceptions.
Within a single mind, they are able to know the minds of all sentient beings.
One's own mind and the minds of others— these two are not discriminated.
Recalling past lives for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges,
one likewise does not discriminate between what came before and what came after.
Able to reach immeasurable lands, manifesting various supernormal powers,
yet within body and mind, there is no thought of weariness.
Discerning and knowing all phenomena, their eloquence in joyful exposition is inexhaustible.
Throughout incalculable eons, he has revealed the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Having crossed to the further shore of wisdom, he is skilled in understanding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
he constantly teaches sentient beings that there is no grasping and no conceptual proliferation.
Skillfully knowing the dharma of causes and conditions, one remains far removed from the characteristics of the two extremes;
knowing that this is the cause of affliction, one also knows it to be the cause of purification.
Through faith and understanding of the dharma of causes and conditions, one is then free from all false views.
All phenomena belong to causes and conditions; they have no fixed foundation.
The view of self and the view of the Buddha, the view of emptiness and the view of birth-and-death, as well as the view of nirvana—none of these views exist at all.
With immeasurable light of wisdom, knowing the true mark of all phenomena,
free from darkness and unobstructed— this is the practice of the path to bodhi.
This vehicle is called the Mahāyāna, the inconceivable vehicle.
It fully accommodates all sentient beings, yet its capacity remains inexhaustible.
Among all vehicles, this vehicle is the foremost;
such is the Great Vehicle, for it is able to give birth to all other vehicles.
The other vehicles have limited measure and cannot receive all beings;
only this Unsurpassed Vehicle can receive all sentient beings.
If one practices this immeasurable Great Vehicle of space, [it is like the great ocean that receives all rivers].
Toward all sentient beings, He harbors no heart of stinginess.
Space is immeasurable And possesses neither form nor color;
The Mahāyāna is likewise thus— Immeasurable and without obstruction.
If all sentient beings were to ride upon this Great Vehicle, one should contemplate the characteristics of this vehicle:
it is vast and expansive, capable of containing much.
Even if one were to speak of the merits of the Great Vehicle for immeasurable and incalculable eons, [they would remain inexhaustible].
And those who ride upon this vehicle cannot be fully enumerated.
If a person hears this sutra, or even upholds a single verse,
they shall forever be liberated from all calamities and attain the place of peace and security.
Those who reverently contemplate this sutra, after casting off this present body,
shall never fall into the evil realms, but will always be born among gods and humans.
Even in future times of degeneration, if they should hear this sutra, [they shall likewise attain such merit].
I bestow upon them all the prediction of enlightenment, that they shall ultimately attain the path of Buddhahood.
