“Regarding what this devaputra has said:
‘That the body does not arise and the mind does not arise—this is the foremost, firm, and powerful diligence. O Brahmā!

I recall that in all my past lives, I practiced with firm and resolute vigor, observing the precepts and the dhūta ascetic practices; I made offerings and showed reverence to my teachers and elders; I dwelt in secluded places, single-mindedly and diligently practicing the Way, reciting and studying the scriptures until I was widely learned; I took pity on sentient beings and provided them with their necessities;
and I persevered with earnest vigor in all difficult practices and austerities—yet the Buddhas of the past did not grant me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because I abide in body, speech, and mind, giving rise to the marks of diligence, Brahmā!
Because I later attained the firm and vigorous diligence as described by the Devaputra, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."

"Therefore, Brahmā! If a bodhisattva wishes to swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment, they should cultivate such firm and powerful diligence, which is to say: not giving rise to the conceptual mark of diligence toward any phenomena."
“World-Honored One!
What is the mark of diligence that does not arise?
The Buddha said:
“Diligence that is equal to the emptiness of the three periods of time is called diligence that does not give rise to signs.
“World-Honored One,
what is diligence that is equal to the emptiness of the three periods of time?”
The Buddha said: "The past mind has already ceased; the future mind has not yet arrived; the present mind does not abide.
If a dharma has ceased, it will not arise again; if it has not yet arrived, it lacks the characteristic of birth; if it does not abide, it abides in the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)."

Furthermore, true reality (dharmatā) is also without arising; if a phenomenon is without arising, it has no past, future, or present. If there is no past, future, or present, then its nature has been eternally unarisen from the very beginning. This is called the vigor of the equality of the three times as empty, which enables a bodhisattva to swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment.

“Brahmā! When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), they are able to thoroughly comprehend all dharmas as having nothing to be relinquished; this is called dānapāramitā.
To thoroughly comprehend all dharmas as being without outflows (anāsrava) is called śīlapāramitā.
To thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without harm is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
to thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without arising is called the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
to thoroughly understand that all phenomena are equal is called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
To thoroughly comprehend all phenomena as being without discrimination is called the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva comprehends in this manner, then regarding all phenomena there is neither increase nor decrease, neither correctness nor error.
Although this bodhisattva practices giving, he does not seek its karmic reward;
although he maintains the precepts, he has no attachment to them;
although he practices patience, he realizes the emptiness of both the internal and the external.
Though practicing diligence, he knows the characteristic of non-arising;
though in meditative concentration, he has no point of reliance;
though practicing wisdom, he grasps no characteristics.
“Brahmā! When a bodhisattva accomplishes such patience in the Dharma, although they manifest all modes of conduct, they remain undefiled.

Such a person attains the mark of equality regarding the world; they are not shaken by gain or loss, defamation or praise, renown or insignificance, pleasure or pain, because they have transcended all worldly dharmas.”

Neither exalting oneself nor disparaging others, neither rejoicing nor grieving, neither wavering nor indolent, free from dualistic mind and detached from all conditions, one attains the non-dual Dharma;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings who have fallen into the view of duality, one gives rise to great compassion, assumes a body for their sake, and teaches them.

"Brahmā! This is called the first firm and powerful diligence: namely, attaining the patient acceptance of non-self, emptiness, and dharmas, while giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings and taking on a body for their sake."

When these characteristics of firm and resolute diligence were being spoken, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Buddha bestowed upon them their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), declaring that they would all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and each achieve the Way of the Buddha in different lands, all bearing the same name: Firm Diligence (*Dṛḍhavīrya*).
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is like the great dragons: when they wish to send down rain, they rain upon the great ocean; [the Buddha’s teaching is likewise]."
"These bodhisattvas are also like this, raining down the great rain of Dharma upon the minds of bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
As you have said, the reason the great dragon kings do not send rain upon Jambudvīpa is not out of stinginess, but simply because that land is incapable of receiving it.
Why is this? The rain poured by the great dragon falls in torrents as thick as chariot axles.

If it were to rain, Jambudvīpa—including its cities, towns, villages, mountains, forests, ponds, and pools—would all be swept away like drifting jujube leaves; therefore, the great dragon does not pour down heavy rain upon Jambudvīpa.

In this way, Kāśyapa, it is not out of a sense of stinginess that these bodhisattvas do not rain down the rain of Dharma upon other sentient beings; rather, it is because their vessels are incapable of receiving such teachings as these.
Therefore, these bodhisattvas rain down such inconceivable, unsurpassed rains of Dharma solely upon the hearts of the bodhisattvas, which are like a vast ocean of profound wisdom.
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean can receive heavy rains falling like chariot axles without increasing or decreasing, so too it is with these bodhisattvas:
whether for one kalpa or even for a hundred kalpas, whether listening or teaching, their Dharma remains serene, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as when the myriad rivers flow into the great ocean, they all become of one salty taste;
so it is with these bodhisattvas: though they hear various teachings and various discourses, they are all able to believe and understand them as having the single taste of emptiness.”
In the preceding fascicle, from the passage beginning "At that time, Mahākāśyapa... according to the Dan edition, this is the twenty-first chapter, the "Parable of the Ocean. "Kāśyapa!
Furthermore, it is like the great ocean, which is clear, pure, and free of defilement; when turbid water flows into it, it immediately becomes clean.
These bodhisattvas are also like this, purifying the stains of all fetters, resentments, and afflictions."
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean is profoundly deep and bottomless, so too are these bodhisattvas.

Because they are able to contemplate and enter into immeasurable dharmas, they are called ‘profoundly deep’; because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom them, they are called ‘bottomless.’”

“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean collects immeasurable waters, so too do these bodhisattvas collect immeasurable dharmas and immeasurable wisdom; for this reason, it is said that the minds of bodhisattvas are like the great ocean.”
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean accumulates all kinds of immeasurable precious treasures, so too it is with these bodhisattvas:
they enter various gateways to the Dharma, gather the treasures of all dharmas, and through practicing various paths, they give birth to immeasurable accumulations of the treasures of the Dharma.”
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, it is like the great ocean, which possesses three kinds of jewels:
first, those of little value; second, those of value; and third, those of incalculable value.

The Dharma taught by these bodhisattvas is likewise: according to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, they cause them to attain liberation—some attaining liberation through the Hīnayāna, some through the Madhyamayāna, and some through the Mahāyāna.
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore,
just as the great ocean gradually becomes deeper,
so too do these bodhisattvas gradually become deeper in their orientation toward sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse;

so too it is with these bodhisattvas—they do not harbor the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor do they harbor minds of stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distracted mindfulness, or delusion, nor do they harbor views of a self, a person, or a sentient being.”

“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, it is like when the kalpa comes to an end and is consumed by fire: the various small ponds, rivers, streams, and springs dry up first, and only then does the great ocean finally vanish.

When the True Dharma is extinguished, it is just the same: the True Dharma of all conditioned practices and minor paths is exhausted first, and only then does the True Dharma of the great ocean-like mind of a bodhisattva perish.”
Kāśyapa! These bodhisattvas would rather lose their bodies and lives than abandon the true Dharma.
Do you think that these bodhisattvas abandon the true Dharma?
Do not form such a view. Kāśyapa!

It is like that great ocean which contains a vajra-jewel named "Gatherer of All Jewels. Even when the seven suns arise and the fire reaches as far as the Brahma-world, this jewel is neither burned nor lost; it is transferred to another great ocean in a different direction.
If this precious jewel were in this world, it would be impossible for the world to burn;
these bodhisattvas are also like this: when the True Dharma is extinguished and the seven false dharmas emerge, they will even go to other worlds.
What are the seven?
First, the treatises of non-Buddhists;
second, evil associates.
Third, the wrongful application of the Dharma;
fourth, mutual provocation and disturbance;
fifth, entering the thorny forest of false views.
Sixth, they do not cultivate merit;
seventh, there is no attainment of the Way.

When these seven evils arise, these bodhisattvas know that sentient beings cannot be saved, and thus they go to Buddha-lands in other directions, never ceasing to see Buddhas, hear the Dharma, transform sentient beings, and increase their roots of goodness.
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the great ocean is the refuge for immeasurable sentient beings, so too are these bodhisattvas;
sentient beings rely upon them and thereby obtain three kinds of happiness:”
The pleasure of humans, the pleasure of devas, and the pleasure of nirvāṇa. “Kāśyapa,
it is also like the great ocean, which is salty and undrinkable;”
"These bodhisattvas are also like this; no māras or non-Buddhists can swallow them up or extinguish them.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The great ocean, though deep, may still be measured; these bodhisattvas, however, cannot be measured.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The atoms within a trichiliocosm may still be counted and known, but the merit of these bodhisattvas is immeasurable and cannot be numbered."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this matter, spoke in verse:
"Just as the great ocean can receive all waters, Never reaching a point of fullness, So too are these bodhisattvas:
Constantly seeking the benefit of the Dharma without weariness."
Just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams, And they all return to it without increase or decrease, So too are these bodhisattvas:
Upon hearing and receiving the profound Dharma, there is neither increase nor decrease.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean does not admit turbidity, and all turbid waters that flow into it become completely pure, so too are these bodhisattvas: they do not admit any defilement of afflictions.
Furthermore, just as the great ocean has no shore or bottom, so too are these bodhisattvas;
their merit and wisdom are immeasurable, such that all sentient beings cannot fathom them.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean has no distinctions, and the hundred rivers that flow into it all become of one taste, so too are these bodhisattvas: the Dharma they hear and receive is of a single characteristic.
Just as the great ocean comes into being not for the sake of a single sentient being alone,
so too are these bodhisattvas, who universally give rise to the mind of enlightenment for the sake of all.

Just as there is a sea-treasure named "Gatherer of Jewels," and because of this treasure there exist all other jewels, so too is the Bodhisattva a treasury of jewels; from the jewel of the Bodhisattva, all jewels emerge.
Just as the great ocean produces three kinds of jewels, yet this great ocean has no discrimination, so too is the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma:
using the Three Vehicles to deliver beings without distinction between self and other.
Just as the great ocean gradually deepens, so too are these bodhisattvas;
for the sake of sentient beings they cultivate merit, dedicating it toward the profound *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Furthermore, just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, so too are these bodhisattvas:
having generated the pure mind and the vow for enlightenment, they do not harbor the defiled minds of śrāvakas.
Just as the great ocean contains a firm and solid jewel, Named "Gatherer of All Jewels," which is never consumed even when the kalpa ends in flames,
And is carried away to other buddha-fields in another direction.
When the True Dharma is extinguished, it is likewise so: those who are firm and diligent can uphold the Dharma;
knowing that sentient beings cannot be saved, they proceed to the presence of the Buddhas in other lands.

When the trichiliocosm is about to perish, and the fire calamity is about to arise to incinerate heaven and earth, the myriad rivers and streams dry up first; at that time, the King of Waters dries up last.
Those who practice the Lesser Vehicle are also like this: they perish first when the Dharma is about to end;
the Bodhisattvas, being courageous and not sparing their own bodies, protect and uphold the True Dharma until it finally comes to an end.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma-jewel within the mind does not perish;
dwelling in this Dharma with a profoundly pure mind, one practices the Path through these wholesome dharmas.
A hundred thousand sentient beings rely upon the ocean, yet the ocean was not formed for the sake of a single being;
likewise is the bodhisattva’s resolve, for the purpose of liberating all sentient beings.
The vast oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions may still have their measures fathomed,
but the path traversed by these bodhisattvas cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Kāśyapa, you should know that among all bodhisattvas, those with minds of courageous diligence and dedication who vow to become Buddhas and deliver sentient beings— there is not even one equal to them, let alone one superior.
This mass of merit-treasures is like a great ocean; this is a worthy field of merit for offerings;
this is the supreme Great King of Physicians, able to heal the illnesses of all sentient beings.
He is the refuge of the world and its protector, the island, the lamp, and the ultimate path;
he can bestow the eye of wisdom upon the world, and with that eye, one may drink the nectar of immortality.
He is the Dharma King of all in the world; he is Śakra’s wisdom of decisive judgment;
he is the Brahmā King practicing the four dhyānas; he is the one capable of turning the Brahma-wheel of Dharma.
This is the Greatly Wise Guide of the World, who shows all the crooked paths and the true, correct Way;
this is the one who is courageous and able to destroy Māra; this is the one who is pure and eliminates afflictions and defilements.
Cultivating pure dharmas like the full moon, His radiant brilliance is as exalted as the sun;
His wisdom transcends all like Mount Sumeru, Like dense clouds raining down ambrosia.
He is fearless like a lion; his mind is tamed and supple like a king of elephants;
he is like a mountain of diamond, which no outsider can destroy.
This is pure like water; this possesses the ferocity of a great fire;
this is like the wind, without obstruction; this is like the earth, incapable of being moved.
This uproots the root of the self and pride; this is like a medicinal tree, free from discrimination;
this maintains pure precepts like a lotus flower; this is unstained by worldly dharmas.
This is like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in ten million billion kalpas;
this is what is meant by knowing how to repay the Buddha’s kindness, and this is what is meant by not severing the lineage of all Buddhas.
This is the practice of great compassion through diligent effort; this is the transcendence achieved through loving-kindness and sympathetic joy;
this is the mind capable of relinquishing the five desires; this is the constant seeking of the precious wealth of the Buddha-dharma.
This practice of giving is most supreme; this upholding of pure precepts has no equal;
this patience is heroic and peerless; this diligent exertion is free from weariness;
this practice of meditative concentration possesses supernormal powers, enabling one to reach immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Constantly seeing the Buddhas and hearing their teachings, they explain them to others exactly as they have heard them.
Knowing the paths traversed by sentient beings, they act according to their inclinations and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties;
this is called skillfully knowing the power of expedient means, and it is the place where the lamp of wisdom is lit to achieve salvation.
They are able to skillfully know that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
they are able to decisively comprehend the characteristics of causes and conditions, remaining free from the view of self and delighting in equanimity.
This is the ability to correctly contemplate all phenomena: from where they come and to where they go;
skillfully knowing that all phenomena have no coming or going, they eternally abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without movement.
Seeing that all conditioned phenomena are empty, one increases great compassion to rescue sentient beings;
because sentient beings give rise to manifold sufferings through deluded thoughts, one practices the Path for the sake of delivering them.
Ordinary beings discriminate between "self" and "what belongs to self," Practicing various kinds of false views;
One who can clearly understand the true reality of phenomena Preaches the Dharma in order to sever all such views.
Taking the impermanent as permanent and the impure as pure, taking the non-self as self and suffering as pleasure—
because ordinary beings are thus inverted and greedily attached, the prior limit of birth and death cannot be known.
One who can know that this arises from inversion— That there is no self, no person, and no sentient being— Should thus cultivate the true path: Impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity.
Kāśyapa, you should know that these bodhisattvas possess the various merits I have praised;
their practice is inexhaustible, like taking up a single speck of dust from the great earth.
If one has resolved upon bodhicitta without regression, then even the offerings of the three thousandfold world-system,
or any other offerings superior to these, should all be presented as worship to such a person.
If a person resolves their mind to become a Buddha, they thereby pay respect and make offerings to me;
they have likewise paid respect and made offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

16. Chapter on Establishing the Dharma (4). Chapter Sixteen: Establishing the Dharma; Chapter Twenty-two: The Prophecy for the Devaputra Dan Tianzi. At that time, the Brahma-king Siyi addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
“You should request the Tathāgata to protect and mind this sutra, so that it may be widely disseminated during the final five-hundred-year period of the later age.”
Mañjuśrī said: "What do you think?
Regarding this sutra, does the Buddha have any dharma, any teaching, any demonstration, or anything to be protected and remembered?"
Siddhārtha said: "No, Brahmā. "Brahmā! [he continued].

Therefore, you should know that all dharmas are without speech, without demonstration, and without protective mindfulness; these dharmas can ultimately never be extinguished, nor can they be protected by mindfulness.
If one wishes to protect this Dharma, it is as if one wishes to protect and keep in mind empty space. Brahmā!
If a bodhisattva says:
"To have something to receive as the Dharma" is a statement that is not the Dharma. Why is this?
Because it transcends all verbal discourse.
This is called the bodhisattva’s delight in being free from contention. Brahmā!
If there is a bodhisattva who, within this assembly, forms such a thought:
"When it is said that 'this Dharma is now being taught,' one should know that such a person is not actually listening to the Dharma.
Why is this? For it is by not listening to the Dharma that one truly listens to the Dharma."
Brahmā asked, "For what reason do you say that one who does not listen to the Dharma is truly listening to the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied:
"When the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without leakage, this is listening to the Dharma.
Why is that? If one is without leakage regarding the six internal sense bases, then within forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, one is truly listening to the Dharma."

At that time, thirty-two thousand devaputras in the assembly, five hundred bhikṣus, three hundred bhikṣuṇīs, eight hundred upāsakas, and eight hundred upāsikās, having heard what Mañjuśrī had spoken, all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, they spoke thus: "So it is, so it is!"
"Mañjuśrī! As you have said, it is precisely those who do not listen to the Dharma who truly listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the bodhisattvas who had attained patience, saying:
"Do you not listen to this sutra?
The bodhisattvas replied,
"As we listen, we listen by means of non-listening."
He asked again:
"How do you know this Dharma? They replied:
"To claim that what is not known is known.
He asked again:
"For what reason have you attained what is called 'attainment of patience'?"
He replied, "Because all dharmas are unattainable, we are said to have attained patience. Siyi said:
"What is meant by 'practicing in accordance with this Dharma'?
He replied, "It is practicing in accordance [with it] precisely because one does not practice in accordance [with it]."
He asked again:
"Have you clearly understood and mastered this Dharma? They replied:
"All dharmas are clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated, for there is neither 'self' nor 'other.
At that time, there was a son of heaven in the assembly named Viśuddhalakṣaṇa, who said to the Brahmā Sahāmpati:
"If there were anyone who merely heard this sutra but the Buddha did not grant them a prediction of enlightenment, I would myself bestow upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? Because this sutra does not subvert cause and effect; it can give rise to all wholesome dharmas, destroy the enmity of Māra, and bring one away from all hatred and attachment. It can cause the minds of sentient beings to attain purity, and enable those who have faith to find universal joy and eliminate all anger and resentment.

This sutra is that which all virtuous persons practice; this sutra is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind; this sutra is that which all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world together guard and protect. Because this sutra leads decisively to the stage of non-retrogression; because this sutra does not deceive and leads to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); because this sutra is truly able to cause sentient beings to attain all Buddha-dharmas; because this sutra can turn the wheel of Dharma; because this sutra can eliminate doubt and regret; because this sutra can open the path of the sages; those seeking liberation should listen well to this sutra; those wishing to obtain dhāraṇīs should uphold it well; those seeking merit should explain it well; and those who delight in the Dharma should contemplate it well.

This sutra can bestow happiness leading to nirvana; this sutra cannot be interrupted by Māras, non-Buddhists, or those who cling to acquisitions; this sutra should receive offerings from those who can follow its meaning; this sutra can cause those of sharp faculties to rejoice, and it can cause those possessed of wisdom to be filled with gladness.
This sutra can bestow wisdom upon people because it causes them to leave behind all views; this sutra can bestow knowledge upon people because it destroys ignorance.

The phrasing and sequence of this sutra are well-expounded; this sutra is ultimately expounded in accordance with the meaning. This sutra provides great benefit by expounding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); this sutra is what those who love and delight in the Dharma treasure and cherish. This sutra is that which those with wisdom cannot part from; this sutra is a great treasury for those who practice giving; this sutra is a pool of coolness for those afflicted by the heat of suffering. This sutra can cause the minds of the compassionate to become equanimous; this sutra can cause the indolent to become diligent; this sutra can cause those with distracted thoughts to attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*); this sutra can grant the light of wisdom to the foolish.
"Brahmā! This sutra is that which all Buddhas hold in the highest esteem.
When the Devaputra Viśuddhalakṣaṇa preached this Dharma, the trichiliocosm shook violently.
The Buddha then praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent,
O Devaputra!"
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Has this devaputra previously heard this sutra in the presence of the Buddhas of the past?
The Buddha said,
"This devaputra has already heard this sutra in the presence of sixty-four billion Buddhas."
After forty-two thousand kalpas have passed, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Ratnavyūha; his land shall be called Bahuratna.
During that interval, there will be Buddhas who appear, all of whom he shall serve and from whom he shall hear this sutra.

Brahmā! These bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits who have attained the patience of the Dharma within this assembly, shall all be reborn in the land of Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, the Devaputra Viśuddhalakṣaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I do not seek awakening, I do not wish for awakening, I do not crave awakening, I do not delight in awakening, I do not dwell upon awakening, and I do not discriminate awakening. How then does the Tathāgata grant me this prediction?”
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"It is as if one were to throw grass, wood, stalks, joints, branches, and leaves into a fire, and say to them: 'Do not burn!'"
"Do not be thus! If it were otherwise because of these words, such a thing would be impossible,
O Devaputra!"

The Bodhisattva is also like this: although they do not take delight in or become greedily attached to bodhi, it should be known that such a person has already received the prediction of enlightenment from all Buddhas. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva does not rejoice, does not delight, does not crave, and does not cling, yet does not fail to attain awakening, then they will certainly receive from all Buddhas the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
At that time, five hundred bodhisattvas in the assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We now do not seek awakening, do not aspire to awakening, do not delight in awakening, do not crave or cling to awakening, do not dwell upon awakening, and do not discriminate awakening.”

Having spoken these words, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, he immediately beheld eighty-four thousand Buddhas in the direction of the zenith, who bestowed upon him the prophecy of his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, five hundred bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha,
saying: "It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!"
What the Tathāgata has spoken is most excellent and wonderful!
That which is called a bodhisattva not seeking, not aspiring for, not coveting, not delighting in, and not attaining bodhi, yet receiving the prediction of Buddhahood from all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
We now behold eighty-four thousand Buddhas in the direction above, and each of those Buddhas has bestowed upon us the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Chapter 17: The Gods’ Praise (4). Chapter 17: The Gods’ Praise (in the *Dān* [Chinese] edition, this is Chapter 23: The Tathāgata’s Divine Mantra). At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One will protect and keep this Dharma in mind, so that in the future age, during the final five hundred years, it may be widely proclaimed and disseminated throughout this Jambudvīpa and cause it to endure for a long time;
furthermore, may all sons and daughters of good family who possess great adornment hear it.”
Even if various demonic activities arise, they will not follow after Māra, nor will the followers of Māra find any opportunity;
because they uphold this sūtra, they shall never fall back or lose their *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Buddha said to Mañjuśrī: "So it is, so it is!
Listen well now!"
In order that this sutra may endure for a long time, I shall now expound for you the incantations for summoning the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others.
